summary: Content fidelity is strong. Coverage is complete: all 40 slides appear exactly once, headed "SLIDE n", in order, with no duplicated, missing or invented slides. Speaker-note substance is carried almost in full — every timing structure, protocol phase, role, case fact, finding, grade, KPI and vigilance timeline in the notes reaches the transcript, including the items speakers most often lose (the 820.180(c) exemption not carrying over, the 50-minute lobby delay and its "refusal is grounds for suspension" observation, the major going to the legal manufacturer rather than the subcontractor, the grade-3-plus-repeat arithmetic behind grade 4, the "teaching aid, verify before relying on any cell" caveat on slide 32, and the flipchart callback from slide 3 to slide 35). Clause and citation accuracy is clean: I checked every ISO clause and sub-clause, every 21 CFR reference, every MDR article and annex, every regulation number, standard designation and date against the source and found no alteration, transposition or mis-statement, and no fabricated figure, statistic or citation anywhere in the 40 slides — so there are no blocking findings. What remains is eleven minor items: two genuine substance losses (slide 20 drops the FDA and notified-body "What escalates" column; slide 11 drops "symptom fixes" and the over-one-year open CAPA), three case specifics from slide 22 that are never spoken anywhere (three weeks past calibration, four months since install, four years since supplier audit), one internal inconsistency (slides 26 and 28 direct 3 minutes of table work against the 2-read/3-discuss rhythm the speaker announced on slide 21 and used on slides 22 and 24), an asserted speaker name where slide 1 carries a placeholder, and four small unsupported editorial assertions or glosses (slides 3, 9, 19, 26, 31, 35). Verdict: pass, with those fixes recommended before recording.

findings.problem: The speaker's actual lexicon has been stripped out. His characteristic latinate qualifier stack is everywhere in the corpus and almost absent from the draft (corpus vs draft counts): "robust" 21/0, "ensure/ensuring" 19/0, "appropriate" 19/0, "significant" 24/1, "comprehensive" 13/0, "essential" 13/1, "adequate" 12/1, "crucial" 10/0, "rigorous" 9/0, "proactively" 7/0, "meticulous" 5/0, "navigate" 2/0, "leverage" 1/0. Where the corpus writes "Strong data governance is non-negotiable... Establish clear policies right from the start, prioritizing data quality through rigorous collection, curation, cleaning, and annotation processes" and "it is essential to provide a clear and concise explanation," the draft writes concrete Anglo-Saxon prose with no qualifiers at all: "Grade honestly against notified body or MDSAP definitions, time every retrieval, and interview your operators" (slide 36). The draft reads as a cleaner, tougher writer than the man in the corpus.
findings.fix: Reintroduce his qualifier habit at roughly corpus density (~1.5 per 100 words across robust/ensure/appropriate/comprehensive/adequate/crucial/rigorous). E.g. slide 36 should read closer to "It is essential that the grading is performed rigorously against notified body or MDSAP definitions, that every retrieval is timed, and that a robust set of operator interviews is conducted to ensure that practice is being assessed and not just documentation." Slide 31's "Governance is what stops the architecture quietly decaying" should be "A comprehensive governance structure is essential to ensure that the architecture does not degrade between certification cycles."

findings.problem: The draft has an epigram habit the corpus does not have: nearly every paragraph is landed with a balanced, quotable one-liner. "Every box on this diagram is a place where readiness is either real or it is not" (12); "if you cannot reconstruct the lot on the day, everything else is theory" (11); "a finding is a finding and a finding gets closed, while falsification is a career event and a company event" (18); "Your certificate travels to your critical suppliers, and so does your audit" (25); "a procedure owned by a committee is a procedure that drifts" (31); "a variant form is a second process wearing the same document number" (31); "a metric that is reported but never trended is just another record in the file" (34); "a humbling Tuesday you chose costs far less than the Tuesday your notified body chooses" (36); "whoever is sitting at reception at 08:10 on a Tuesday is part of your quality system" (15). The corpus never does this. Its paragraph closers are flat and explanatory: "In essence, this Impact Assessment is your demonstration to the FDA that you've proactively and comprehensively evaluated the downstream effects of your planned evolution for the device."
findings.fix: Cut the aphorism from each of these paragraphs and replace with a flat restatement of the requirement. Slide 12: instead of "Every box on this diagram is a place where readiness is either real or it is not," write "It is important to note that each of these areas requires appropriate documented evidence, and a gap in any one of them will be identified during an audit." Slide 36: instead of the "humbling Tuesday" line, "It is highly recommended that manufacturers conduct this exercise internally, as identifying these gaps on your own schedule is significantly less costly than having a notified body identify them for you." Keep at most one epigram in the whole deck.

findings.problem: Systematic antithesis. "rather than" appears 27 times in the draft against 3 in the corpus, plus 6 uses of the "X and not Y" construction against 2. It is the draft's signature move and it is not his: "a permanent state rather than a project you schedule" (1), "by reference rather than restating" (6), "a pattern rather than a prediction" (7), "the backbone of readiness rather than one more document in the stack" (8), "as a written protocol rather than as a reaction" (16), "a working room rather than as an idea" (16), "an operating document rather than a reference document" (33), "readiness rather than the appearance of compliance" (34), "Readiness is produced by routines and not by heroics" (34), "Readiness is a state and not an event" (37).
findings.fix: Reduce to 3 or 4 uses across the whole deck and rewrite the rest as plain positive statements. Slide 16's "the first 60 minutes on site have to run as a written protocol rather than as a reaction" becomes "it is essential that the first 60 minutes on site are governed by a documented protocol." Slide 16's "the back room is stood up as a working room rather than as an idea" becomes "the back room is established with the appropriate personnel, systems access, and printing capability in place." Slide 34's "Readiness is produced by routines and not by heroics" becomes "Readiness is the product of a consistent operating rhythm, which is outlined on the left."

findings.problem: Mechanical over-imitation of one formula. "X include:" with a mid-sentence colon followed by an inline comma list is used 19 times (corpus: 5). More importantly the construction itself is an invention. In the corpus the colon appears only where a real bulleted list follows ("This includes:", "Some general examples include:"), and inline lists are introduced with "including" and no colon: "including establishment registration, device listing, Quality System Regulation soon to be the QMSR, Medical Device Reporting or MDR for adverse events..." The draft instead writes sentences like "The logistics agreed in that room include: the rooms themselves, printing, system access, your photo and sample policy, and the route by which..." (17) and "The remaining markets most of you deal with include: Brazil under RDC 665/2022..." (6). This reads as parody of his list habit, and "which include:" (4 uses) appears nowhere in the corpus.
findings.fix: Delete the colon in every inline instance and use "including" or a plain relative clause. Slide 17: "The logistics agreed in that room include the rooms themselves, printing, system access..." Slide 6: "The remaining markets most of you deal with include Brazil under RDC 665/2022..." Reserve the colon form for the three or four places where you genuinely intend a list (slide 1's "4 things", slide 34's KPI targets), and cut total uses of the formula to roughly 6-8.

findings.problem: The signature segue is used at nearly every section boundary. "So now that we have [established/a baseline understanding of]... we can [move on to/begin to look at]..." appears 9 times (slides 5, 8, 10, 13, 17, 20, 21, 27, 36) against 3 in the corpus, and "So now you may be asking" a further 3 times against 1. At that rate it stops reading as a habit and starts reading as a template, e.g. slide 20 "So now that we have a baseline understanding of the day and of the 72 hours behind it, we can begin to look at the vocabulary you will need" arriving one slide after slide 17's "So now that we have established how the first hour should run, we can move on to who is actually running it."
findings.fix: Keep the formula at 3 or 4 uses on the genuine section walls (slide 5, slide 8, slide 21, slide 30) and vary the rest using other transitions that are actually in the corpus: "Before we get too deep into..." (slide 9 already does this correctly), "I would like to take a moment to discuss...", "Alright great, so you told me about X, but how do I...", or simply "The next area we would want to consider is...". Reduce "So now you may be asking" to one use.

findings.problem: Pronoun discipline is inverted. The corpus's default grammatical subject is the third-person "manufacturers" (70 uses, 6.2 per 1,000 words) with "your device" for the specific: "It is critical that manufacturers assess the risk...", "Manufacturers should be aware that this template was made mandatory...". The draft uses "manufacturer(s)" only 31 times (2.4 per 1,000, under 40% of corpus density) while "you" rises to 9.5 per 1,000 (corpus 5.1) and "your" to 7.3 (corpus 3.8). Whole stretches are second-person coaching where he would write about manufacturers: "you should check your own contract for that number, while for the Medical Device Single Audit Program, or MDSAP, you should expect around 15 calendar days for the plan" (19), and "Give yourself a point for each one you could defend with evidence today" (35).
findings.fix: Convert roughly half the second-person sentences to his third-person default while keeping "your device / your site / your notified body" for the possessive. Slide 19: "The response plan must be submitted to the notified body within its stated window, and manufacturers should verify that period against their own contract, while for MDSAP manufacturers should expect approximately 15 calendar days for the plan." Slide 10's "every item in that middle column is something you should be able to produce within minutes" becomes "...is something manufacturers should be able to produce within minutes for the product the auditor has just selected."

findings.problem: Short punchy fragments used for effect, which the corpus never does. Draft average sentence length is 28.3 words against the corpus's 22.5, but the draft carries 24 sentences of 7 words or fewer against the corpus's 13 — and the corpus's short ones are all best-practice imperatives ("Document these efforts thoroughly.", "Report these metrics comprehensively, including confidence intervals."), never rhetorical beats. The draft's are: "That model is gone." (4), "The history here takes one breath." (5), "It is an undocumented decision." (11), "Mechanics first." / "Focus second." (15), "That is the back room." (17), "This company had read that sentence. Its subcontractor had not." (24), "Auditors follow product." / "The first hour sets the verdict." / "Findings are root-cause problems." (37).
findings.fix: Fold each fragment back into the sentence that follows it. Slide 4: "For 20 years most of us prepared for audits, and the calendar told us when to start. That model is gone." becomes "For 20 years most manufacturers prepared for audits on a schedule, and the calendar dictated when that preparation began; however, that model is no longer adequate." Slide 5: delete "The history here takes one breath." entirely and open with "I would like to take a moment to walk through the history here." Slide 11: "It is an undocumented decision." becomes "...the failure is rarely the absence of a system, but rather an undocumented decision."

findings.problem: The most conspicuously non-corpus passage in the deck. "Annex IX section 3.4 says that the notified body may audit your suppliers and subcontractors unannounced. This company had read that sentence. Its subcontractor had not." This is a three-beat dramatic reveal with a withheld punchline — a construction that appears nowhere in over 11,000 words of corpus, and one that reads as generic polished presentation writing rather than as him.
findings.fix: Rewrite in his flat setup register, as he does at the top of the Presentation_Slides endoscope section: "I would like to take a moment to discuss the second case, which deals with an area that manufacturers frequently overlook. Annex IX section 3.4 permits the notified body to audit your suppliers and subcontractors unannounced. It is important to note that while this manufacturer was aware of that provision, its subcontractor had not been made aware of it, and that is where this case begins."

findings.problem: The takeaways slide is five telegraphic headline sentences followed by imperative fragments: "Readiness is a state and not an event." / "Auditors follow product." / "The first hour sets the verdict." / "Findings are root-cause problems." / "A global QMS is one process with local annexes." followed by "A script, a roster, defined roles, and named deputies, because reception is part of your Quality Management System" — which is not even a sentence. The corpus's analogous position (Common_Submission_Pitfalls conclusion, Data_Integrity conclusion) is full explanatory prose: "As we wrap up discussing best practices, I want to reiterate that the 510(k) pathway for innovative AI-powered devices requires more than just demonstrating technological feasibility or simple equivalence; it requires a rigorous, well-documented approach..."
findings.fix: Convert each of the 5 into a full explanatory sentence with a subject and a verb, in his conclusion register. E.g. "The first point I want to reiterate is that readiness is a permanent state and not a scheduled event. Manufacturers should operate on the assumption that auditors will arrive tomorrow morning at 08:00, and should therefore build appropriate routines into the quality system rather than preparing for a specific date." And: "The third point is that the first hour largely determines the outcome. It is critical that manufacturers have a documented reception script, a 24/7 roster, defined response roles, and named deputies, as reception personnel are a functional part of your Quality Management System."

findings.problem: Number style is inconsistent with the corpus and internally. The corpus writes small numbers as numerals almost without exception ("1 of 3 risk levels", "2 warning letters", "only 7 FDA cleared disposable endoscopes", "5 comprising of disposable components", "14 presubmission packages"); only two spelled-out number words appear in all 11,000 words. The draft correctly uses numerals in most places ("3 questions", "4 things", "2 documents") but then spells out roughly 20 others, sometimes within the same sentence: "a company that has all four and a company that has three of them" (30), "Four deviations had been closed locally" (25), "a Form FDA 483 carrying four observations" (27), "There are three questions for your tables" (28), "Two notified body auditors presented their credentials" (22), "Two failures recur" (10), "Readiness Self-Test: Ten Questions" (35).
findings.fix: Convert every spelled-out number to a numeral: "all 4 and a company that has 3 of them", "4 deviations had been closed locally", "a Form FDA 483 carrying 4 observations", "There are 3 questions for your tables", "2 notified body auditors presented their credentials", "2 failures recur", "Readiness Self-Test: 10 Questions". Slide 12's "The first stop is the device history record" is fine; the issue is only the number words.

findings.problem: "Three good sites, three honest procedures, and one certificate, and the gap in this case sat between them rather than inside any one of them." This is a rhetorical triple used as a slide opener, with spelled-out numbers and the "rather than" antithesis attached. The corpus opens case-style material factually: "The company is the legal manufacturer of..." or "Since 2015, the FDA has placed a significant focus on..."
findings.fix: "The company in this case operated 3 well-run sites, each with its own documented procedures, all under a single certificate. It is important to note that the gap identified here sat in the interfaces between those sites, and not within any individual site."

findings.problem: "Let us make this concrete." The corpus uses the contracted, often unapostrophed form throughout — "lets dive in", "let's unpack exactly what the FDA means by it", "So let's start with our first Myth" — and never the formal "Let us".
findings.fix: "So let's make this concrete." Or, closer to his usual scene-setting move: "I would like to take a moment to discuss a common scenario." (his exact wording at corpus SLIDE 7).

findings.problem: "Mechanics first." (slide 15) and "Focus second." (slide 15) are two-word ordinal fragments used as inline headers. The corpus's enumeration habit is the full-clause form he uses for the PCCP elements: "The First Element is the Description of the Modification", "The Next Element is the Modification Protocol", "The Third and Oftentimes Overlooked Element is the Traceability Table". The draft gets this right on slide 31's tiers and then abandons it here.
findings.fix: "The First Area I want to discuss is the Mechanics of the Audit." and "The Next Area is the Focus of the Audit." Same fix applies to slide 17's "That is the back room." — expand to "That responsibility belongs to the back room."

findings.problem: "An investigator who sees a candid record with closed actions behind it is reassured, one who sees a glossy record with nothing in it isn't." A balanced two-clause antithesis joined by a comma splice, with the verb elided in the second half. This is a literary construction, and the elision-plus-splice is more copy-edited than anything in the corpus, which joins clauses with "however", "additionally", "furthermore" and full semicolons.
findings.fix: "An investigator who reviews a candid record with closed actions behind it will be reassured by what they see. However, an investigator who is handed a record that contains nothing of substance will draw the opposite conclusion."

findings.problem: The opening formula is very slightly off. The corpus opens all three webinars with "Hello and thank you Laura for that introduction and thank you to those who are joining us for today's presentation"; the draft drops the named introducer: "Hello and thank you for that introduction and thank you to those who are joining us for today's presentation." Separately, the self-introduction is vague where his is always quantified — corpus: "I have prepared and submitted 14 presubmission packages in the last 2.5 years"; draft: "My own background is in device quality and regulatory work, and I have sat on the manufacturer's side of the table for audits and inspections." The draft uses "I" 65 times (5.0 per 1,000 vs corpus 2.9) but almost entirely as a facilitator ("I want to highlight", "I am going to ask") and never in his signature first-person war-story mode with hard numbers.
findings.fix: Restore the named introducer ("thank you Laura for that introduction", or whoever is introducing). Quantify the credential in his style: "I have supported manufacturers through 11 notified body and FDA audits in the last 4 years, and I have sat on the manufacturer's side of the table for each one of them, which is why this topic matters to me." Consider adding one concrete first-person anecdote mid-deck, as he does at corpus Myth 9 ("I once worked with a startup who was so eager...").

findings.problem: Density check on the requested stock phrase, plus a copy-editing tell. "It is important to note that" appears 7 times against 4 in the corpus; the full family (note/know/remember/highlight) is 12 in the draft against roughly 8 in the corpus, or 0.92 vs 0.71 per 1,000 words. That density is slightly high but broadly acceptable and does not read as parody. What does read as edited, however, is that the draft rotates the variants to avoid repetition (note, then know, then remember, then note) whereas the corpus happily repeats the identical phrase within a few paragraphs. Related mechanical drift: 21 semicolons against the corpus's 7, and straight apostrophes throughout ("don't", "FDA's") where the corpus is consistently typographic ("don't", "FDA's").
findings.fix: Leave the count roughly as is but stop rotating: let "It is important to note that" carry 8 or 9 of the 12 and drop "It is important to remember" (3 uses, and the corpus only has it once, contracted, as "it's important to remember that"). Cut about half the semicolons to "however" or a full stop, and normalise apostrophes and quotation marks to the curly forms used in the corpus.

summary:
Needs work. The draft gets the skeleton of his voice right — the opening and closing formulas are correct and appear only where they should, the "So now that we have..." and "It is important to note that" habits are present, the "The First Tier is... The Next Tier is... Finally the Last Tier is" enumeration on slide 31 is a good match for his PCCP-element pattern, "Stipulated through Regulation 2023/607", "In regards to FDA", "I will always caution manufacturers", "This is by no means an exhaustive list" and the general-list caveats all land, and it correctly avoids the obvious AI tells (no em-dash asides beyond his own two en-dash pairs, no "In today's rapidly evolving landscape", no "It's worth noting").

The problem is one level down, in the sentences themselves. Two things went wrong in opposite directions. First, over-imitation: three formulas are used at two to four times corpus density — the "So now that we have established..." segue 9 times against 3, and, worse, an "X include:" mid-sentence colon 19 times, a construction the corpus never uses at all (he only puts a colon before a genuine bulleted list, and writes inline lists with "including" and no colon). Second, and more serious, the prose register is not his. His actual lexicon is bureaucratic-consultant — "robust" 21 times, "ensure" 19, "appropriate" 19, "significant" 24, "comprehensive" 13, "crucial" 10, "rigorous" 9 — and the draft has 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0 of those. In their place it has an epigram habit he does not have ("a variant form is a second process wearing the same document number"; "Your certificate travels to your critical suppliers, and so does your audit"), a "rather than" antithesis used 27 times against his 3, and punchy fragments used for rhythm ("That model is gone."; "Mechanics first."; "This company had read that sentence. Its subcontractor had not."). Pronoun discipline is also inverted: his default subject is third-person "manufacturers" at 6.2 per 1,000 words, the draft's is 2.4, while "you/your" nearly doubles into second-person coaching.

The net effect is that the draft reads as a better, tighter, more quotable writer than the man in the corpus. The formulas are a costume over someone else's prose. Fixing it means reinstating his latinate qualifiers, deflating the paragraph-closing aphorisms, converting the fragments and the slide 37 headlines into full explanatory sentences, and moving the default subject back to "manufacturers".

findings.problem: The speaker's most distinctive voice feature is entirely absent: the first-person war story. The corpus carries at least seven ("I actually recently worked with a manufacturer who was asked to provide clinical performance data...", "I once worked with a startup who was so eager to ensure FDA left with a positive impression that during the meeting they casually discussed and proposed testing far exceeding the regulatory requirements", "I have prepared and submitted 14 presubmission packages in the last 2.5 years", "Each of these myths listed are taken from real accounts from manufacturers I have worked with in my past", "Trust me when I say that FDA will never stop a company from going above and beyond"). Across 41 slides and 14,175 words the draft has zero. Its closest approaches are depersonalised into third-party citation: slide 14's "Practice reports from 2026 gap assessments are consistent here, in that certified-only firms often had no signed, element-by-element label release record" and slide 30's "The assumptions that certified firms made include...". He does not talk about "practice reports"; he talks about a firm he sat with.
findings.fix: Convert two or three of the depersonalised observations into named anecdotes in his construction. Slide 14 should read something like "I recently worked with a firm who was certified to ISO 13485 and had been through MDSAP twice, and when I asked to see their label release record for a single lot, what I got back was one checkbox that said 'labels verified'. Trust me when I say that an investigator will not read that as a five-point examination." Slide 30's assumptions list and slide 31's findings list want the same treatment on at least one item each.

findings.problem: Every date in the deck is in day-month-year international format, 41 times: "2 February 2026", "23 February 2022", "24 May 2022", "15 October 2024", "4 December 2025", "16 December 2025", "27 May 2026", "21 July 2026", "24 July 2026", "the town halls on 14 January and 1 April 2026". The corpus uses US format: "made mandatory for device submissions starting on October 1, 2023", and elsewhere "In January of this year", "Since 2015", "In 2024". Zero US-format dates appear in the draft. For a US FDA regulatory speaker addressing a US audience this is the most conspicuous non-him tell in the deck.
findings.fix: Convert all 41 to month-day-year: "February 2, 2026", "February 23, 2022", "May 24, 2022", "October 15, 2024", "December 4, 2025", "May 27, 2026", "July 21, 2026", "the town halls on January 14 and April 1, 2026".

findings.problem: British spellings appear five times. Slide 31: "mark the 3 findings you recognise, and by recognise I mean the ones where you are not confident a record exists today." Slide 13: "servicing records must be analysed to decide whether what you are holding is in fact a complaint." Slide 16: "filed in the service log without ever being analysed as a possible complaint." Slide 31: "service reports never analysed for complaints". The corpus is uniformly US: "recognize" four times ("it is easy to recognize why", "most senior regulatory team members will recognize this", "I recognize it is messy"), plus "utilize", "organized", "minimize".
findings.fix: "recognise" to "recognize" (both instances on slide 31); "analysed" to "analyzed" on slides 13, 16 and 31.

findings.problem: The opening formula drops the named introducer. The draft reads "Hello and thank you for that introduction and thank you to those who are joining us for today's presentation." All three corpus openings name her: "Hello and thank you Laura for that introduction and thank you to those who are joining us joining today's presentation." The draft also silently repairs the corpus's characteristic doubled "joining us joining today's presentation" into clean "joining us for today's presentation" — a copy-edit of the one rough seam in his most-repeated sentence.
findings.fix: "Hello and thank you Laura for that introduction and thank you to those who are joining us for today's presentation." Restore the name; keeping the smoother "joining us for" is defensible, but the name is not optional.

findings.problem: The five takeaway headings are title-cased epigrams built on antithesis and chiasmus, a register that appears nowhere in the corpus: "Renaming Is Not Compliance, Evidence Is", "The Investigator Opens Your Risk File, Not Your Manual", "Management Review And Audit Records Are Inspection Documents Now". The body under them is written to match: "FDA does not care what you call the file." and "the record that shows a problem being worked is worth far more than the record that shows no problems at all." The corpus's own summary headings are flat and functional — "Elements to Include in a PCCP Submission:", "The First Element is the Description of the Modification", "The Third and Oftentimes Overlooked Element is the Traceability Table" — and its closing paragraphs run as prose, not aphorism.
findings.fix: Flatten to his heading register and unwind the epigrams, e.g. "The First Takeaway is that Renaming a File is Not Compliance" over a body of "It is important to note that FDA is not evaluating what you have titled the file. The agency is evaluating whether the record exists, whether it contains the content the regulation requires, and whether it demonstrates that the process was effective." Same treatment for the other four.

findings.problem: Throughout the deck, lists the corpus would set out as bullets are flattened into inline semicolon runs, which reads far more copy-edited than his prose. Slide 21: "the rewritten examples include: no documented process for risk management in product realization under Clause 7.1; feedback and postmarket surveillance not used as inputs to risk management; design, process, or supplier changes not evaluated for risk and impact before implementation; the same or similar significant deficiencies not corrected since the last inspection; and nonconforming product distributed with injury potential...". Slides 35 and 36 do the same at greater length. There are roughly 22 such constructions. The corpus uses the semicolon only to join two independent clauses, almost always with "however" ("This program is entirely voluntary; however, it can provide manufacturers with clear regulatory guidance"; "I recognize it is messy; however, this was taken directly from FDA's guidance document") — never as a list separator. His lists break to hyphen bullets or numbered items every time.
findings.fix: Break these into bullets after the colon, as in the corpus. Slide 21 becomes "The rewritten examples include:" followed by "- No documented process for risk management in product realization under Clause 7.1", "- Feedback and postmarket surveillance not used as inputs to risk management", and so on. Reserve the semicolon for the "; however," construction.

findings.problem: The self-introduction is a convoluted construction unlike anything in his register: "I work as a regulatory consultant on device quality systems, and where I sit relative to this transition is on the industry side of it, supporting gap assessments, remediation programs, and firms preparing for and hosting inspections under the new framework." "where I sit relative to this transition is on the industry side of it" is a writerly inversion; the corpus openings state the topic and move on, and where he establishes standing he does it plainly and by count ("I have prepared and submitted 14 presubmission packages in the last 2.5 years").
findings.fix: "I work as a regulatory consultant supporting device quality systems, and I have spent the last two years running gap assessments and remediation programs and sitting with manufacturers through inspections under this new framework."

findings.problem: The list-introducing colon formula is over-used to the point of a tic. "include:" appears 22 times in 14,175 words against 5 times in the corpus's 11,242 — roughly three and a half times the corpus density — and clusters badly: slides 34, 35 and 36 carry it seven times between them ("the deliverables include:", "That last 20% includes:", "the targets include:", "it includes:", "That work includes:", "What it does need includes:"). Combined with the semicolon flattening, the deck announces a list every few sentences.
findings.fix: Cut to roughly eight or nine uses. Where the list is short, write it as prose in his manner ("The deliverables for Phase 0 are a charter, a named executive sponsor, a scope and applicability statement, and one named owner for every QMS process"); keep the explicit "include:" plus bullets only where the list is genuinely long and reference-grade.

findings.problem: The section-transition formula is used ten times against four in the corpus — about twice the density — and the strain shows in the variants: slide 12 "So now that we have established which 4 provisions carry the FDA-specific weight, we can begin to look at the first of them", slide 14 "So now that we have a baseline understanding of the records content, we can move on to the one production control FDA wrote out in full", slide 26 "So now that we have a baseline understanding of how a QMSR inspection actually runs, we can move on to what you need to build", slide 27 "So now that we have established what a crosswalk can and cannot do for you, we can begin to look at the rows themselves", slide 33 "So now that we have established what the 2026 gap assessments keep finding, we can move on to...". By slide 33 it reads as a tic rather than a transition.
findings.fix: Keep it at the four or five genuine section boundaries — slides 8, 11, 17 and 26 — and vary the rest using his other transitions: "Alright great, so...", "Before we get too deep into...", "I would like to take a moment to discuss...", or a plain "The next area I want to discuss today is...".

findings.problem: A cluster of clipped imperative aphorisms punchier than anything in the corpus. Slide 22: "Write candidly, close the loop, and do not redact what you hand over." (a three-beat imperative triple). Slide 36: "Put it there and keep it there, because FDA reads the minutes." Slide 14: "Don't let that be your record." Slide 34: "Stop polishing the quality manual until those are done." Slide 13: "Mark them in advance of the inspection, and never redact what you hand over. A confidentiality marking isn't a shield against review." The corpus's nearest equivalents are single and much softer — "Don't make this selection in isolation.", "Document these efforts thoroughly." — and his advice normally arrives inside a longer hedged sentence ("I always recommend a less is more approach when considering how much information should be openly shared during these meetings").
findings.fix: Absorb them into sentences. Slide 22: "I always recommend that manufacturers write these records candidly, close the loop on every action opened, and refrain from redacting anything that is handed over." Slide 36: "It is important to note that FDA reads the minutes, so this belongs in your management review inputs and it belongs there permanently." Slide 14: "It is important to note that a single 'labels verified' checkbox will not survive a review of this requirement."

findings.problem: Whimsical and literary asides that do not occur in the corpus. Slide 34: "Phase 4 is Verify, and it is the phase programs quietly skip" and "That phase does not close, which is rather the point of it" — "which is rather the point of it" is a dry British construction. Slide 29: "Terminology is where most of the room has already spent an argument or two". Slide 39: "if nothing else from today survives the drive home, these are the ones that should". Slide 19: "The message there is not a subtle one: top management owns risk" and "which is worth sitting with for a moment". Slide 9: "The left column here is the reassurance, and the right column is the warning." His own asides are blunter and more practical ("so first off, I would like to apologize for the overall look of this flowchart, I recognize it is messy").
findings.fix: Plain them out. Slide 34: "Phase 4 is Verify, and it is the phase most programs skip." and "Phase 5 does not have a closing date, and that is intentional." Slide 19: "What that tells you is that top management owns risk management under this program." Slide 9: "The items in the left column should provide some reassurance, while the items on the right are where manufacturers are getting caught."

findings.problem: Balanced antithesis used as a closing beat, four times. Slide 26: "a crosswalk is where you start, and it is not where you finish." Slide 30: "200 undifferentiated rows is not a transition plan." Slide 38: "Those are commitments now rather than intentions." Slide 39: "the record that shows a problem being worked is worth far more than the record that shows no problems at all." The corpus never builds a sentence on this kind of symmetry; its summary sentences are declarative and slightly over-stuffed ("In essence, this Impact Assessment is your demonstration to the FDA that you've proactively and comprehensively evaluated the downstream effects of your planned evolution for the device.").
findings.fix: Unwind each into a declarative. Slide 26: "It is important to note that the crosswalk is a starting point for this work, and manufacturers should not treat the completed mapping as the end of the transition." Slide 30: "A list of 200 rows with no priority attached to any of them will not function as a transition plan." Slide 38: "These are now documented commitments rather than intentions."

findings.problem: Contraction discipline is inconsistent between the two matching exercise debriefs, and one is stiffer than his register allows. Slide 25 reads "Let us bring it back together and hear from 2 tables"; slide 32 reads "So let's come back together." The corpus is consistently contracted in these first-person hinges: "So with that said, lets dive in", "So let's start with our first Myth", "let's unpack exactly what the FDA means by it".
findings.fix: Slide 25 becomes "So let's bring it back together and hear from 2 tables, 90 seconds each."

findings.problem: Rhetorical triples of adjectives, which the corpus does not use. Slide 32: "The 40 procedures feel urgent because they are visible, countable, and satisfying to close out". Slide 21: "the risk you identified, the record where the decision lives, and the evidence that the control worked" is a mannered three-part parallel, introduced with the equally mannered "and it is worth rehearsing before anyone is standing in your conference room". The corpus's triples are always concrete nouns from the regulation ("access, illumination, and allow observation"; "bench testing, animal testing, and even sometimes clinical testing"), never abstract adjectives assembled for cadence.
findings.fix: Slide 32: "The 40 procedures feel urgent because they are easy to see and easy to count." Slide 21: "So when an investigator says show me how risk informed this decision, there are 3 things that answer needs to contain, and manufacturers should rehearse this before anyone is standing in their conference room. The first is the risk you identified, the second is the record where the decision was made, and the third is the evidence that the control was effective."

findings.problem: The corpus habit of writing small numbers as digits ("1 of 3 risk levels", "only 7 FDA cleared disposable endoscopes") has been pushed past the point where it reads naturally, particularly where "both" is the word he would use. Slide 4: "those 2 movements in opposite directions". Slide 7: "the 2 phrases are not interchangeable". Slide 9: "which catches firms who assumed the 2 could be merged". Slide 18: "remove the 2 features of QSIT that manufacturers had learned to prepare for". Slide 20: "Model 2 has only 2 uses". The corpus itself writes "both types of endoscopes", "both of which are readable", "both clinicians and patients".
findings.fix: Use "both" where the reference is to a pair already named: "those two movements in opposite directions", "the two phrases are not interchangeable", "firms who assumed the two could be merged", "remove both of the features of QSIT that manufacturers had learned to prepare for".

findings.problem: Slide 23 is a single undivided 315-word paragraph running from "These are verbatim excerpts from the first Warning Letters..." through "...you will need to respond in the same vocabulary within 15 business days." Slides 37 and 40 do the same at 218 and 201 words. The corpus does contain one 266-word block (the pre-submission anecdote), but that is its outlier; his normal paragraph runs 60 to 130 words and he breaks for each new idea, often with a bare heading ("PCCP", "Data Bias", "The Foundational Role of Data").
findings.fix: Break slide 23 into three paragraphs at the natural seams — the two letters and their inspection dates; the citation format including the TM-112 and Clause 7.4.1 examples; and the adulteration sentence plus the 15-business-day response point. Do the same on slides 37 and 40.

findings.problem: Four invented variants on his hedge formula appear alongside the genuine ones, and they are near-misses rather than his phrasing: slide 35 "It is worth remembering that these are archetypes rather than categories", slide 5 "it is worth knowing that FDA's frequently asked questions page describes that rule as issued 31 January 2024", slide 19 "which is worth sitting with for a moment", slide 21 "it is worth rehearsing before anyone is standing in your conference room". The corpus uses "It is important to note that", "It is important to know that", "it's important to remember that" and "It should be noted that" — never "it is worth" anything. Worth recording, though, that the overall hedge density is right: the four genuine forms appear 14 times in 14,175 words against 11 times in the corpus's 11,242, which is 9.9 versus 9.8 per ten thousand words. That is a match, not over-imitation, and "It is important to note that" specifically lands at 4.9 per ten thousand against his 5.3. The problem is the four counterfeits, not the count.
findings.fix: Swap each to a corpus form: "It is important to remember that these are archetypes rather than categories", "it is important to know that FDA's frequently asked questions page describes that rule as issued January 31, 2024", and on slide 21 simply "and manufacturers should rehearse this answer before anyone is standing in their conference room".

summary: Needs work, though the underlying imitation is better than the finding count suggests. The structural skeleton is right: the opening formula sits only on slide 1 and ends with the corpus's own unapostrophised "So with that said, lets dive in"; slide 41 closes with both of his closing formulas in the correct order ("So with that said, it is easy to recognize why..." then "This concludes the presentation portion of this discussion. I want to thank each of you who attended, and I welcome any questions you may have at this time"). The classic AI tells are genuinely absent — no em-dash asides at all (zero, against five in the corpus), no "Let's dive into", no "rapidly evolving landscape", no bulleted fragments. Most importantly, the hedge density is correct rather than parodic: the "It is important to note / know / remember / It should be noted" family runs at 9.9 per ten thousand words against the corpus's 9.8, and "It is important to note that" alone at 4.9 against 5.3. Anyone expecting that phrase to be the failure mode here should check the arithmetic first. What actually breaks the voice is five things. Every date in the deck is in international day-month-year form, 41 times, where his one dated reference reads "October 1, 2023". Five British spellings ("recognise" twice, "analysed" three times) sit in a US FDA talk. His signature move — the first-person war story, seven of them in the corpus — is completely missing, replaced by depersonalised "practice reports indicate" constructions. Slide 39's takeaways are title-cased epigrams built on chiasmus ("Renaming Is Not Compliance, Evidence Is"), a register he never uses. And about 22 lists that he would set out as bullets have been flattened into inline semicolon runs, making the deck read as more copy-edited than he is; his semicolon is almost exclusively the "; however," joint. Beneath those, the prose keeps reaching for a literary beat he does not have: balanced antitheses as closers ("a crosswalk is where you start, and it is not where you finish"), clipped imperative triples ("Write candidly, close the loop, and do not redact what you hand over"), and dry asides ("which is rather the point of it", "the phase programs quietly skip", "if nothing else from today survives the drive home"). Two formulas are over-pulled at roughly twice corpus density — the "So now that we have established X, we can begin to look at Y" transition at ten uses, and the list-introducing "include:" at 22 — and four counterfeit hedges ("it is worth remembering / knowing / sitting with / rehearsing") have been coined where his four real ones would do. Pronoun discipline is sound throughout: "we" for speaker-plus-room, "you/your device/your site" for the manufacturer addressed, "manufacturers" in the third person, matching the corpus pattern, with no "You should ensure that you" coaching. Fix the dates, the spellings, the semicolon lists and slide 39's headings, and graft two real anecdotes onto slides 14 and 30, and this passes.

findings.problem: The draft ends the gap-assessment explanation with an invented regulatory claim: "they measured 'procedure updated' instead of 'record produced', and an investigator doesn't sample procedures." Nothing in slide 30's on-screen text or notes says this, and it contradicts the deck elsewhere: slide 23 quotes Warning Letters that cite the firm's own procedures by document number ("Your firm's Risk Management procedure TM-112 does not define how risk management activities are performed"), and slide 31 cites Linemaster's corrective action procedure as "silent on cause determination and effectiveness" and Koven's supplier procedure. Slide 30's own bottom row also scores 40 procedures that cite "21 CFR 820.30".
findings.fix: Cut "and an investigator doesn't sample procedures" and use the note's actual point: "The column that matters is 'record sampled and what it lacked', because CP 7382.850 tests whether the process works, not whether the procedure reads well."

findings.problem: Two whole crosswalk rows are never spoken. 820.25 Personnel to Clause 6.2 (delta: "Competence, training effectiveness proportionate to risk, records") is absent entirely, and so is 820.50 Purchasing controls to 7.4.1-7.4.3 (delta: "Risk-proportionate criteria, monitoring and re-evaluation; supplier audit reports reviewable; 4.1.5 outsourced processes"). Purchasing is the number-two cited area on slide 24, so its crosswalk row is load-bearing. Also dropped: the 820.40 delta ("'Document' means establish, implement, maintain (Clause 0.2); records readily identifiable and retrievable") and the 820.70 deltas contamination control (6.4.2) and software validation (4.1.6, 7.5.6, 7.6).
findings.fix: Add one sentence each: personnel moves to 6.2 with training effectiveness proportionate to risk; purchasing controls move to 7.4.1 through 7.4.3 with risk-proportionate criteria, monitoring and re-evaluation, reviewable supplier audit reports and 4.1.5 outsourcing. Add the 0.2 "document" point and contamination control 6.4.2 / software validation to the existing 820.40 and 820.70 sentences.

findings.problem: The "When it is used" column of the seven-type table is almost entirely dropped. The draft lists which types take Model 1 or 2 but never says non-baseline surveillance requires a prior FDA inspection or MDSAP audit classified NAI or VAI and no active MDSAP enrolment, that compliance follow-up follows a prior inspection or audit that "led to regulatory action", that for-cause follows "a signal, issue or complaint: recalls, MDRs, prior observations, RRA follow-up", that a Specific Product Risk Assignment follows "a specific product risk identified by FDA", that PMA preapproval requires that "validations must be complete first", or that baseline surveillance also applies where "risk factors indicate a need" (the draft says only "New sites with no inspection or audit history").
findings.fix: Add a short clause to each type as it is named, e.g. "non-baseline surveillance, where a prior FDA inspection or MDSAP audit came back NAI or VAI and the site is not enrolled in MDSAP", and for Model 2 say "baseline surveillance, meaning no FDA inspection or MDSAP audit history, or risk factors that indicate a need; and PMA preapproval, for which your validations must be complete before FDA arrives."

findings.problem: Nine of the twelve terminology rows are never spoken. The draft covers only DMR to medical device file and DHR to medical device or batch record. Missing: "Establish (define, document, implement)" to "Document (establish, implement, maintain), Clause 0.2" with FDA's note that "document" is the broader word; "Manufacturing material" to "Process agent (7.5.2)", assessed and controlled commensurate with risk; "Nonconformance" to "Nonconformity"; "CAPA" to correction, corrective action (8.5.2), preventive action (8.5.3) with separate triggers and records; "Complaint files" to feedback (8.2.1), complaint handling (8.2.2), reporting to regulatory authorities (8.2.3); "Statistical techniques" to analysis of data (8.4); "Reasonably accessible; readily available" to "Readily identifiable and retrievable (4.2.5)" with remote records next working day or two; and the manual-scope rename to cite 21 CFR 820 and ISO 13485:2016.
findings.fix: Add a 4-5 sentence pass down the table naming at least the establish/document change (Clause 0.2), manufacturing material to process agent (7.5.2), the CAPA split, complaint files to 8.2.1/8.2.2/8.2.3, statistical techniques to 8.4, and readily identifiable and retrievable (4.2.5) with the next-working-day expectation.

findings.problem: Three crosswalk rows are dropped without the notes authorising it. 820.80/820.86 Acceptance to 7.4.3, 8.2.6, 7.5.8 (delta: "Purchased product verification proportionate to risk; status identification") is never mentioned; 820.100 CAPA to 8.5.2, 8.5.3 with 8.4 and 8.2.1 (delta: "Correction, corrective and preventive action split; effectiveness verified") is never mentioned on this slide; and 820.140-820.160 Handling and storage to 7.5.11 and 7.5.9.2 with 820.10(d) (delta: "Risk-based preservation; consignee records where 7.5.9.2 applies") is never mentioned. The draft's substitute sentence ("the remaining rows hold fewer surprises") tells the room to ignore them.
findings.fix: In the closing sentence of slide 28, name them: acceptance activities move to 7.4.3, 8.2.6 and 7.5.8 with verification proportionate to risk and status identification; CAPA splits into correction, corrective action 8.5.2 and preventive action 8.5.3 with effectiveness verified; handling and storage become risk-based preservation under 7.5.11, with consignee records where 7.5.9.2 applies.

findings.problem: The Warning Letter quotation is introduced as what the slide "reads" but is misquoted: the source text is "Failure to maintain records of the review, evaluation, and investigation for any complaints ... as required by 21 CFR 820.35(a)", and the draft silently closes the ellipsis into "for any complaints, as required by 21 CFR 820.35(a)." The draft also drops the attribution, saying only "a Warning Letter issued on 21 July 2026" where the source names Koven Technologies.
findings.fix: Say "the Koven Technologies Warning Letter of 21 July 2026 reads, in part, 'Failure to maintain records of the review, evaluation, and investigation for any complaints' ... 'as required by 21 CFR 820.35(a).'" Keep the elision audible.

findings.problem: The draft announces "I am going to read it word for word" and then reads FAQ #8 with the source's ellipsis removed: the source is "... are not maintained in the QMSR. ... Such records are maintained in the regular course of business ...", so material between those sentences is omitted while the reading is presented as complete.
findings.fix: Either keep the elision ("and then, skipping a line, 'Such records are maintained in the regular course of business ...'") or change the framing to "I am going to read the operative sentences."

findings.problem: The note's argument is inverted. The note says FDA called a one-to-one comparison "cumbersome and not useful (Comment 18). It was half right." The draft renders this as "FDA is correct that the comparison is not where this work ends" - which both concedes FDA's point and attributes to FDA a statement it did not make (FDA said not useful, not "not the end point"). The "half right" pushback (a crosswalk is useful, as a starting point) survives only in the following clause.
findings.fix: "FDA said a one-to-one comparison would be cumbersome and not useful. I think that is half right: a crosswalk is where you start, it is just not where you finish."

findings.problem: The draft tells participants the answers are in their own materials - "The model observations are in your Facilitator Guide" (slide 25) and "the reasoning on both of them is written up in the session materials in your pack" (slide 32). The source says "Model answers are in the Facilitator Guide" and "the answers are in the Facilitator Guide", and slide 2 lists the participant materials as Handout, Exercise Pack and Workbook only - no Facilitator Guide. The room will look for a document it does not have.
findings.fix: Say "the model observations are in my Facilitator Guide and I will walk them at the debrief" on slide 25, and on slide 32 "the reasoning on both cards is in the Facilitator Guide, so come and find me for it".

findings.problem: Half of the vendor-data caveat is dropped. The note flags two circulating figures - "about 90 percent of observations cite ISO clauses" and "almost all classified VAI" - as vendor compilations rather than FDA publications. The draft names only the 90 percent claim.
findings.fix: Add the second one: "and the claim that almost all of these inspections were classified Voluntary Action Indicated - both come from vendor compilations of FDA databases, not from an FDA publication."

findings.problem: Two qualifiers on the 820.3(b) superseding terms are dropped. The slide defines rework as applying "before release for distribution; per the medical device file", and the draft lists "rework" bare. (The before-distribution half resurfaces on slide 28; the medical-device-file half is never said anywhere.)
findings.fix: When listing the five superseding terms, say "rework, which FDA defines as work done before release for distribution and in accordance with the medical device file".

findings.problem: The draft fills the slide's "[Name, Title]" placeholder with invented specifics - "My name is Jordan Elder" and "I work as a regulatory consultant on device quality systems" - where the note says only "Introduce yourself in one line and say where you sit relative to this transition" and "Fill in the placeholders on this slide before presenting." The speaker reads this verbatim, so an invented name or title would be stated as fact.
findings.fix: Restore placeholders the speaker must complete: "My name is [Name], [Title], and where I sit relative to this transition is [gap assessments / remediation programs / QMSR-era inspections you have been part of]."

findings.problem: A list is mis-signposted. The draft reads four assumptions (notified body depth, templates carrying UDI, label release, audit reports staying private), then says "The last item on that list is the one that does the damage, which is that they measured 'procedure updated' instead of 'record produced'" - an item it never read out. The fifth source bullet is "Measured 'procedure updated' instead of 'record produced'".
findings.fix: "And the fifth assumption is the one that does the damage: they measured 'procedure updated' instead of 'record produced'."

findings.problem: The purchasing row loses its second finding. The slide's evidence cell reads "Same questionnaire for contract sterilizer and office supplies; critical supplier re-approved on scorecard"; the draft gives only the questionnaire half, dropping the scorecard re-approval that slide 22 calls out as never defensible.
findings.fix: "...where the same questionnaire was used for a contract sterilizer and for office supplies, and a critical supplier was re-approved on a scorecard."

summary: Coverage is clean: all 41 slides appear exactly once, headed SLIDE 1 through SLIDE 41, with no duplicates, no gaps and no invented slides. Clause and citation accuracy is also clean - I diffed every CFR section, ISO clause, Federal Register cite, compliance-program part reference (Part I.9, III.1.B(3), III.C, III.D.1-4), FD&C Act section (201, 501(h), 524B, 704(a)(4)) and comment number in the draft against its own slide's source, and found no altered, transposed or mis-stated citation; the seven-type/two-model assignments on slide 20, the element counts on slide 19, the FY2025 483 figures on slide 24 (791; 820.100(a) 279; 820.198(a) 211; 115; 95; 93) and all seven timeline dates on slide 5 are all correct. One blocking problem: slide 30 asserts \"an investigator doesn't sample procedures\", which is in neither the slide text nor the notes and contradicts slides 23 and 31, where Warning Letters cite the firms' own procedures by document number. The remaining findings are substance loss in the table-heavy slides, concentrated in the crosswalk and terminology slides (27, 28, 29), where whole rows - personnel to 6.2, purchasing controls to 7.4.1-7.4.3, acceptance activities, the CAPA split, handling and storage, and nine of twelve terminology pairs - are never spoken, plus the dropped \"when it is used\" column on slide 20, two quotations (FAQ #8 on slide 22 and the Koven letter on slide 13) read with their ellipses silently closed, an inverted \"half right\" argument on slide 26, and an invented speaker name and title on slide 1.

Needs work. The eight chunks are individually competent but do not read as one person talking, and the deck as written cannot be delivered in 90 minutes.

The three most serious problems are structural. First, deliverability: 12,966 words is about 100 minutes of speech before any interaction, against a stated 90-minute slot that also contains 16-20 minutes of table work and a 90-second silent scoring pause. Slides 36-40 hold roughly 9 minutes of material in the 4 minutes slide 2 allots them. Second, the case-study segment is timed three different ways: slide 21 promises a uniform 7-minute rhythm, slides 22 and 24 direct 5-minute table work, slides 26 and 28 direct 3 minutes with no reading time, and the written debriefs each run about three and a half minutes rather than two. Slides 26 and 28 also send the room into discussion and never bring it back, while slides 22 and 24 both have reconvene lines. Third, the seams show in terminology: MDSAP is expanded in full seven separate times, QMSR four, Device History Record four, Device Master Record four, and MDR is silently used for both the EU Medical Device Regulation and Medical Device Reporting.

On continuity, slide 5 opens by claiming to have established what slide 4 only promised; slide 16 spoils Case 1's 50-minute delay in direct contradiction of slide 2's instruction to meet the cases cold; slide 20 spoils Case 4's grade; slide 12 states the signature drill as 60 minutes where every other slide says 30. Three promises are never kept: the flipchart parking lot from slide 1, the "would you change your answer" callback promised on slide 3, and the "hold on to whichever row you raised" instruction from slide 10. Two of the twelve table questions are set and never answered.

On speakability, slides 13, 20, 32, 33, 34 and 35 are narrated tables, each containing sentences of 70 to 107 words carrying twenty-odd numbers, plus colons and semicolons the listener cannot hear and unspeakable citations (GHTF/SG3/N19, EN ISO 13485:2016+A11:2021, SOR/98-282, and a sentence boundary falling between "820.45." and "820.10"). Slide 32 also contains a broken sentence ("and 48 hours", with no referent) and slide 25 describes a five-hour gap as three hours.

Interaction cues are otherwise good, consistently capitalised, on their own lines and genuinely earned, but chunks 4 and 8 use inline parenthetical acronym expansions ("(SMEs)", "(DHR)") that cannot be spoken, and slide-title lines appear in only four of the eight chunks, with slide 7's titles written as full sentences a presenter will read aloud.

The arc does hold: slide 1's promise that readiness is a state rather than a project is the note slide 40 lands on. But the closing sentence is 45 words and inverted, burying the payoff in a trailing clause, and the floor is opened twice.

findings.problem: The script cannot be delivered in its stated slot. The eight files total 12,966 words. At a careful technical pace (130 wpm) that is roughly 100 minutes of continuous speech, before any interaction. Add the stage-directed table work (16-20 minutes across slides 22, 24, 26, 28), the 90-second silent scoring on slide 35, and five show-of-hands pauses, and the deck runs about 120 minutes against Slide 1's promise: "We run 90 minutes straight through with no formal break" and Slide 2's minute-by-minute budget ending at "The final 4 minutes are the takeaways, the 30-60-90 day plan, and any remaining questions." Slides 36 through 40 alone are 967 words plus a take-answers pause, roughly 9 minutes of material in a 4-minute slot.
findings.fix: Cut approximately 3,500 words, concentrated in the narrated tables (slides 6, 13, 20, 32, 33, 35) where the handout already carries the detail, and re-time slide 2 against the cut script. Either widen the closing segment to 10 minutes or move the self-test (slide 35) into the global-QMS segment explicitly.

findings.problem: The case-study clock is promised one way and stage-directed two different ways across the chunk seam. Slide 21 says "every one of them runs on the same 7-minute rhythm: 2 minutes to read the case at your table, 3 minutes to discuss the questions printed underneath it, and then a 2-minute plenary debrief" and "I am going to be strict with that clock." Slides 22 and 24 direct "[TABLE WORK - 5 MINUTES: 2 TO READ, 3 TO DISCUSS. CIRCULATE.]" but slides 26 and 28 direct only "[TABLE WORK - 3 MINUTES. CIRCULATE.]", with no reading time, for cases whose tasks include "draft the opening paragraph of the 483 response." Separately, the debriefs on slides 23, 25, 27 and 29 run 400-460 words each, about three and a half minutes, not two, and the spoken setup before each table-work cue (250-300 words) is not in the 7-minute budget at all.
findings.fix: Make all four cues identical: "[TABLE WORK - 5 MINUTES: 2 TO READ, 3 TO DISCUSS. CIRCULATE.]". Restate the rhythm on slide 21 as a 10-minute cycle (2 setup, 5 table, 3 debrief) so it matches what is actually written, and reconcile that with slide 2's 47-to-76-minute window.

findings.problem: Slides 26 and 28 send the room into table work and never bring it back. Slides 22 and 24 both have a reconvene line, "That is 3 minutes on the discussion, so let me bring us back together" and "That is time, so let me pull us back to the room", but slide 26 ends on "[TABLE WORK - 3 MINUTES. CIRCULATE.]" and the file simply moves to SLIDE 27, and slide 28 stacks "[TABLE WORK - 3 MINUTES. CIRCULATE.]" directly against "[TAKE ANSWERS FROM TWO OR THREE TABLES BEFORE ADVANCING]" with no spoken words between them. The presenter has nothing to say to stop forty people talking.
findings.fix: Add a reconvene sentence after the table-work cue on slides 26 and 28, matching slides 22 and 24, e.g. "That is time, so let me bring us back together.", before the take-answers cue.

findings.problem: The deck's signature drill is stated with two different clocks. Slide 3 opens on "Who here could hand an auditor the complete Device History Record, or DHR, and full traceability for any lot you shipped last month, within 30 minutes?" Slide 12 then says "pick a random lot, start the clock, and see whether you can reconstruct it end-to-end in 60 minutes." Slides 34 ("30 minutes or less to produce the full DHR and traceability for a random lot"), 35 ("within 30 minutes") and 38 ("the 30-minute Device History Record and traceability drill") all go back to 30. Slide 34 then claims "The first row is the one we opened this session with", which is true of slide 3 and false of slide 12. The confusion is worsened by "the first 60 minutes" being used throughout for the arrival protocol, so a listener hears 60 minutes meaning two different things.
findings.fix: Change slide 12 to 30 minutes so the drill is one number deck-wide, and keep "60 minutes" reserved exclusively for the arrival protocol.

findings.problem: Slide 16 spoils Case 1 in direct contradiction of the cold-read rule set on slide 2. Slide 2 instructs: "Please keep the Case Study Workshop Pack closed until we reach the case study section, because those cases land very differently when you meet them cold, which is exactly how they arrive in real life." Slide 16 then says "I want to highlight 1 number before we go on, which is 50 minutes. That is how long the auditors in our first case study sat in a lobby." Slide 22 delivers the same fact as a fresh reveal, "The auditors were finally taken into the building at 09:00, and those 50 minutes are written into the audit report", and slide 23 asks the room to rank findings whose headline it already knows. The same pattern repeats with slide 20's "Case 4 lands on a grade 4" against slide 29's "So now you may be asking how one late report becomes a grade 4 nonconformity."
findings.fix: Delete the 50-minute pre-reveal from slide 16 (keep the laminated-script point, which stands on its own) and cut "Case 4 lands on a grade 4" from slide 20, replacing it with a spoiler-free pointer such as "Case 4 will show you how these grades escalate."

findings.problem: MDR is used for two different regulations without warning, and a listener has no way to tell them apart. Slide 5 establishes "The MDR, which is the European Union's Medical Device Regulation" and slides 6, 13, 22, 24 and 38 all use MDR in that sense. Slide 26 then says "6 had no documented reportability decision under Medical Device Reporting, or MDR", while slide 22 used "an MDR certificate" to mean the European one. Slide 6's "UK MDR 2002" adds a third referent.
findings.fix: On slide 26 say "under the Medical Device Reporting regulation, Part 803" and never abbreviate it to MDR. Reserve MDR for the EU regulation throughout, and on slide 6 say "the UK Medical Devices Regulations 2002" in full.

findings.problem: Terms are introduced as if for the first time repeatedly, the clearest tell that eight writers worked separately. MDSAP is expanded in full seven times: slide 5 "MDSAP, the Medical Device Single Audit Program", slide 6 "The Medical Device Single Audit Program, or MDSAP", slide 13 "MDSAP, the Medical Device Single Audit Program", slide 19 "for the Medical Device Single Audit Program, or MDSAP", slide 26 "a Medical Device Single Audit Program certificate, or MDSAP", slide 28, and slide 36 "MDSAP (Medical Device Single Audit Program)". QMSR is expanded four times (slides 5, 6, 13, 26). Device History Record four times (3, 10, 16, 25). Device Master Record four times (10, 12, 16, 36), where slide 12's "which many of you will know as the device master record" reintroduces it two slides after slide 10 already did. Also doubled: UDI (6, 26), PRRC (6, 19), CAPA (7, 11, 36), QSIT (6, 27), KPI (2, 34), IVDR (5, 6), Quality Management System (1, 6).
findings.fix: Expand each term exactly once, at its first appearance, and use the bare acronym thereafter. The one defensible exception is a deliberate re-anchoring after a long gap, which should be phrased as a reminder ("the DMR, as we called it earlier"), not as a first introduction.

findings.problem: Chunks 4 and 8 use a written parenthetical convention for acronyms that cannot be spoken, while the rest of the deck uses the spoken "X, or Y" form. Slide 16: "the scribe, the runner and the subject matter experts (SMEs) are assigned by name" and "Runners retrieve the Device History Record (DHR), the Device Master Record (DMR) and the validation records". Slide 19: "the Person Responsible for Regulatory Compliance (PRRC)". Slide 36: "Grade honestly against notified body or MDSAP (Medical Device Single Audit Program) definitions". A presenter reading these aloud either stumbles or reads the bracket.
findings.fix: Convert every parenthetical to the deck's spoken form, or delete the expansion where the term is already established: "the subject matter experts", "the device history record and the device master record", "the PRRC", "against notified body or MDSAP definitions".

findings.problem: Slide 32 is a numeric table read aloud, and it is unlistenable. In three paragraphs it delivers roughly twenty day-counts with no structural relief: "30 calendar days ... 30 calendar days ... 5 work days ... 10 days ... 15 days ... 2 days ... those same 10, 15 and 2 day clocks ... sets 10 days and then 30 days ... 10 days ... 30 days ... and 48 hours ... 15 days and 30 days ... 72 hours ... 10 days ... 30 days ... and 72 hours again". It also contains a broken sentence: "The TGA in Australia works to 10 days for a death or serious injury, 30 days for near-adverse events, and 48 hours", where "and 48 hours" has no referent and simply stops. And "does not separately define a public-health threat clock, as Japan does not either" is an awkward double negative.
findings.fix: Narrate three contrasts, not twenty numbers: the shortest clock in the deck (Brazil, 72 hours for a death), the longest (FDA, 30 calendar days), and the fact that some run in calendar and some in working days. Then say "the full grid is in your handout" and go straight to the design rule. Fix the TGA sentence to "and 48 hours for a serious public-health threat", and rewrite the Japan clause as "Neither Health Canada nor Japan defines a separate public-health threat clock."

findings.problem: Slide 20 is a single 230-word paragraph with no breath points, and its core content is arithmetic no listener can follow: "MDSAP grades every nonconformity from 1 to 5 using the GHTF/SG3/N19 method, where direct-impact clauses start at grade 3 and indirect clauses at 1, plus 1 grade where there is no documented process, plus 1 for a repeat, capped at 5." "GHTF/SG3/N19" has no spoken form. The same paragraph also carries "No Action Indicated, Voluntary Action Indicated, or Official Action Indicated", "seizure, injunction, consent decree, and import alert", "minor and major nonconformities" and "suspension or withdrawal of the certificate": five vocabulary sets in one breathless block.
findings.fix: Break into four short paragraphs, one per regime. Say the citation as "the international GHTF grading method" and drop the document number to the handout. Reduce the arithmetic to the worked example the deck actually needs: "a direct-impact clause starts at grade three, and a repeat adds one, which is how Case 4 reaches a four."

findings.problem: Slide 13 contains two sentences that cannot be said in one breath and that read as citation lists rather than speech. The FDA sentence runs about 105 words: "For FDA, the Quality Management System Regulation at 21 CFR 820 adds the general requirements of 820.10, the records requirements of 820.35, which tie complaint and servicing records to unique device identification and to your Part 803 decisions, and the labeling and packaging controls of 820.45, and it sits alongside Parts 803, 806, 807, and 830, covering medical device reporting, corrections and removals, registration and listing, and UDI." It also asks the listener to hold four bare part numbers and then re-map them onto four expansions delivered in a separate parallel list. The MDR sentence is 71 words with six article ranges: "Articles 83 through 86 ... Articles 87 through 92 ... Article 15 ... Articles 10 through 14".
findings.fix: Split each into three sentences of under 25 words, pair every number with its name at the point of mention ("Part 803, which is medical device reporting"), and cut the numbers that carry no teaching weight: 807 and 830 add nothing spoken and are already in the handout.

findings.problem: Slide 6 has three specific speakability failures. First, a sentence boundary falls between two regulation numbers: "which include: 820.10, 820.35, and 820.45. 820.10 carries the general requirements", which read aloud is "eight-twenty-point-forty-five, eight-twenty-point-ten" with nothing to mark the break. Second, five acronyms in one sentence, three of which are never expanded anywhere in the deck: "CE marking is accepted there to 30 June 2028 for certificates issued under the MDD, the AIMDD, or the IVDD, and to 30 June 2030 for certificates issued under the MDR or the IVDR." Third, "it is the harmonised European version, EN ISO 13485:2016+A11:2021, that carries the presumption of conformity", where the "+A11:2021" has no spoken form at all.
findings.fix: Recast as "FDA adds three of its own requirements. The first, at 820.10, carries the general requirements...". Expand MDD, AIMDD and IVDD on first use or replace the list with "certificates issued under the old directives". Say "the harmonised European version of the standard, with its 2021 annex" and leave the full designation to the handout.

findings.problem: Slide 5 opens with a backward reference to something that has not happened. "So now that we have established that readiness is a permanent state, we can begin to look at who can arrive at your site without warning", but slide 4 only promised the case: "This first section deals with why readiness has become a permanent state ... and we turn to 3 different areas to make that case." Nothing has been established; the three areas are slides 5, 6 and 7. The same slide also contains a self-refuting line: "The history here takes one breath", followed by roughly 150 words of history.
findings.fix: Change slide 5's opening to a forward frame: "The first of those three areas is who can arrive without warning, because it is a longer list than most manufacturers assume." Cut "The history here takes one breath" or cut the history to two sentences so the claim is true.

findings.problem: Slides 5 and 6 deliver the same three facts one slide apart, each time as new information. The Annex IX rule: slide 5 "wrote unannounced audits into law under Annex IX, section 3.4, with a minimum of at least once every 5 years per manufacturer"; slide 6 "under Annex IX section 3.4 your notified body must conduct one at least every 5 years." The MDSAP country list, verbatim: slide 5 "covers Australia, Brazil, Canada, Japan, and the United States"; slide 6 "That single audit covers Australia, Brazil, Canada, Japan, and the United States". And the grading escalation: slide 6 "grades 4 and 5 are escalated to the participating regulators within 5 business days"; slide 20 "A grade 4 or 5 is notified to all 5 participating regulators within 5 business days", with slide 6's "Nonconformities are graded 1 through 5" re-introduced on slide 20 as "MDSAP grades every nonconformity from 1 to 5".
findings.fix: Slide 5 owns who can arrive unannounced; slide 6 owns the regulatory dates. Cut the Annex IX five-year rule and the country list from slide 6, referring back instead ("the same Annex IX provision we just looked at"). Cut the grading scale and escalation window from slide 6 and let slide 20 own grading.

findings.problem: Four deck-wide verbal tics make the script read as assembled written prose rather than one person speaking. "So now that we have [established/a baseline understanding of]" opens slides 5, 8, 10, 13, 17, 20, 21, 27 and 36, nine times, and twice in the identical form "So now that we have a baseline understanding of" (slides 8 and 20). "So now you may be asking" appears on slides 10, 17 and 29. "It is important to note/know/remember" and "It should be noted" appear eleven times. And "N things, which include:" appears twelve times (slides 1, 5 twice, 6 twice, 7, 10, 17, 21, 36 among others), a colon the listener cannot hear followed by a list, with "include" used for lists that are actually exhaustive ("has 5 steps, which include").
findings.fix: Keep at most two "So now that we have established" transitions, at the two largest section breaks, and vary the rest ("That is who arrives. Now what they ask for."). Delete every "It is important to note that": the sentence after it is always stronger without it. Replace "which include:" with a spoken lead-in: "There are five steps. First, ...".

findings.problem: Slide-title lines are present in only four of the eight chunks, and one chunk's titles are written as speakable sentences. Slides 6-10, 16-20, 26-30 and 31-35 each carry a title line after the SLIDE marker ("The 2026 Regulatory Snapshot", "The First 60 Minutes", "Three Sites, One Certificate"), while slides 1-5, 11-15, 21-25 and 36-40 carry none. Chunk 16-20 also omits the blank line the other chunks use. Worse, slide 7's internal headings are full sentences with terminal periods, "The First Question is Show Me the Procedure.", "The Next Question is Show Me the Records.", "The Third Question is Show Me It Happening.", which a presenter reading the script will simply say aloud, while slide 9's headings are bare noun phrases that clearly are not meant to be spoken.
findings.fix: Pick one convention and apply it to all forty slides: either no title lines, or a title line on every slide, blank-line separated, in a form that is visibly not speech. Convert slide 7's three sentence-headings to noun phrases ("Question one: the procedure") so they cannot be mistaken for spoken text.

findings.problem: The arithmetic in Case 2's debrief is wrong and an audience member will catch it. Slide 25 says the rewritten agreement is "the direct answer to a 03:00 call that went unanswered until 08:00 CET and produced 3 hours of recorded delay." Three in the morning to eight in the morning is five hours, not three. Slide 24 also sets the arrival at "09:00 local time" in Penang, which is where the 03:00 CET figure comes from, so the timeline is internally traceable and the five-hour gap is unambiguous.
findings.fix: Change to "5 hours of recorded delay", or if three hours is the audited figure, change the call window to "a 03:00 call that went unanswered until 06:00 CET".

findings.problem: The self-test is delivered as two sentences carrying all ten statements, about 150 words, punctuated by semicolons the listener cannot hear. "They cover the ground we have been over all morning: reception has a written script and the 24/7 roster, including deputies and shutdown periods; every production or supplier change in the last year has a documented design and risk impact assessment; ..." then "The remaining statements cover: management review records you could hand to an FDA investigator today; a critical supplier agreement that grants unannounced access to your notified body and regulators and requires deviation notification, in every case; ...". A room being asked to score itself out of ten cannot track ten criteria delivered this way, and "in every case" floating mid-list is unparseable aloud.
findings.fix: Since the ten statements are already in the handout with tick boxes, stop narrating them. Say "The ten statements are in front of you.
