Read them yourself and score honestly" and go straight to the silent-scoring cue. If they must be spoken, number them aloud: "One. Reception has a written script. Two. ...".

findings.problem: Slide 34's KPI list is a 107-word sentence containing eight targets, three of them the numeral zero and two of them percentages: "the targets include: 30 minutes or less to produce the full DHR and traceability for a random lot, 0 procedures past their periodic review date, 0 pieces of equipment in use past the calibration due date, 0 CAPAs open more than 12 months without an approved justification, 100% of staff trained on the current revision before performing the task, 100% of vigilance reports submitted on time, 95% or more adherence to the supplier audit plan, and a quarterly verification of the reception script and the 24/7 roster." A presenter must also silently decide to say "zero" for "0" and "ninety-five percent" for "95%". Slide 33 has the same defect in a 101-word sentence with a nested em-dash aside: "the required data fields - UDI capture under 820.35 is the current example - and the retention periods differ".
findings.fix: Narrate three KPIs and point at the rest: "Three of these matter most: thirty minutes to a full trace, zero equipment past calibration, and one hundred percent of vigilance reports on time. The other five are on the slide." Spell numerals as words throughout so the presenter is not transcribing on the fly, and lift the em-dash aside on slide 33 into its own sentence.

findings.problem: Slide 1 sets up a parking-lot mechanism that is never resumed: "Questions are welcome at any time, and if one belongs to a later section I will park it on the flipchart and come back to it." Nothing in slides 2 through 40 returns to the flipchart for parked questions. Slide 40 opens the floor without clearing it: "Before we open the floor I want to put the question below back to you", then offers a list of frequently asked questions instead. Slide 2 makes a related unfulfilled promise, "that segment is built to carry your questions" about the 20-to-32-minute block, with no cue for questions anywhere in slides 8 through 13.
findings.fix: Add a line at slide 40 before the take-answers cue: "Before we go wider, let me clear the flipchart. There are [N] questions parked on it from earlier." Add a "[PAUSE FOR QUESTIONS]" cue at the end of slide 13 to honour slide 2's promise, or delete that clause from slide 2.

findings.problem: The opening poll's specific promise is not kept. Slide 3 says "I am writing the rough counts from all 3 questions on the flipchart, and we will come back to those numbers near the end of the session when we run the 10-question readiness self-test, at which point I am going to ask whether anybody in the room would change their answer." Slide 35 only gestures at it: "That is worth holding against the flipchart counts from the three questions we opened with, and you'll notice the room reads itself differently once the questions have evidence attached to them." The promised question, would anybody change their answer, is never asked, and no stage direction exists for it. Slide 3's flipchart-writing is itself an unmarked physical action, the only one in the deck without a bracketed cue.
findings.fix: Add to slide 35, after the show-of-hands cue: "Look at the flipchart. On the thirty-minute question we had [N] hands this morning. Has anyone changed their answer?" followed by "[PAUSE FOR SHOW OF HANDS AGAINST THE FLIPCHART COUNT]". Add "[WRITE COUNTS ON FLIPCHART]" to slide 3.

findings.problem: Slide 10 sets a task the room is told to carry into the cases, and the cases never collect it. "Before we take the second half of this table, look down the right-hand column and raise your hand for the row you recognise from your own site. [PAUSE FOR SHOW OF HANDS] Suppliers and change control usually take the most hands, and both of those rows come back in the case studies, so hold on to whichever one you raised." Slides 22 through 29 never refer back to what anyone raised. Slide 23 does cover change control and slide 25 does cover suppliers, but neither says so, so the instruction "hold on to whichever one you raised" is left dangling for nineteen slides.
findings.fix: Add one clause to slide 23 ("this is the change-control row some of you raised on the clause table") and one to slide 25 ("and this is the supplier row; if that was your hand, this case is yours").

findings.problem: Two of the twelve table questions are set and never answered in the debrief. Slide 28 asks three questions; slide 29 answers the first ("training failed because the root cause was structural") and the third ("the answer was Global Regulatory Affairs") but never answers the second, "what a single global complaint process must contain in order to work in Germany, Costa Rica, and the United States at the same time". Slide 29 only recounts what the company happened to build. Similarly, slide 26's first question, "what mindset caused that 40-minute standoff", is never answered on slide 27; the closest thing is the band quote "we are ISO certified, nothing changes", which is offered as a lesson rather than as an answer to the question asked.
findings.fix: Add an explicit answer to slide 29 for question two (a single intake, one reportability decision tree carrying every market's clock, and a shortest-clock triage rule), labelled as such ("On the second question..."), matching the "On the first question" / "The third question" structure already used. Add one sentence to slide 27 answering the mindset question directly before moving to the model response.

findings.problem: The deck opens the floor twice and its final sentence buries the point the opening promised. Slide 40 says "Before we open the floor I want to put the question below back to you", then runs "[TAKE ANSWERS FROM TWO OR THREE PARTICIPANTS BEFORE OPENING THE FLOOR]", then closes with "This concludes the presentation portion of this discussion. I want to thank each of you who attended, and I welcome any questions you may have at this time", reopening a floor already opened. Between those sits the intended landing, which is grammatically inverted and 45 words long: "So with that said, it is easy to recognize why readiness has to be built as a routine rather than as a project for manufacturers who intend to keep a certificate and a global Quality Management System intact through an audit that nobody put on the calendar." The trailing "for manufacturers who intend to..." clause pushes the payoff out of the stress position, so the close does not land slide 1's promise ("why audit readiness has become a permanent state rather than a project you schedule").
findings.fix: Rewrite the close as two short sentences ending on the promise: "Nobody is going to put this audit on your calendar. That is exactly why readiness has to be a routine and not a project." Then go straight to the take-answers cue and delete the second floor-opening. Drop "This concludes the presentation portion of this discussion."

findings.problem: Slide 39 announces it will not be read and then reads it. "I am not going to read this slide to you. What you will find below is the reference list that sits behind everything we have covered today, which runs from the standards themselves through 21 CFR Part 820 and the reporting and registration parts, the EU MDR and IVDR with the relevant Annex IX provision and the MDCG guidance documents, the MDSAP audit approach and its companion document, and the UK and Canadian regulations." That is a 64-word recitation of the list, in a 4-minute closing segment that is already overcommitted. MDCG is also never expanded anywhere in the deck.
findings.fix: Cut to two sentences: "I am not going to read this slide. Everything we have covered today is sourced here, the same list is in your handout with links, so there is nothing to copy down."

findings.problem: Slide 20's backward reference has its direction reversed: "So now that we have a baseline understanding of the day and of the 72 hours behind it." The 72 hours follow the audit, they do not precede it. Slide 14 set it up correctly as "what has to happen in the 72 hours after they leave" and slide 19 as "what your organization does in the following 72 hours". "Behind it" points backwards.
findings.fix: Change to "of the day and of the 72 hours that follow it".

findings.problem: Slide 12 claims primacy for a model the deck has already walked twice. "This diagram is the mental model for the whole session, and I want to take a moment on it because everything that follows assumes it." But slide 7 already established follow-the-product ("pick a single unit, and follow it"), and slides 10 and 11 already walked the same evidence chain row by row, with slide 11 ending on "Here is how those rows connect when an auditor follows a single unit backwards through your quality system." So "everything that follows" is false for a substantial part of what precedes.
findings.fix: Change to "This diagram is the mental model behind the table we have just worked through, and everything in the rest of the session hangs off it."

findings.problem: Slide 29 calls the MDSAP auditing organization a notified body, mixing two regimes the deck has carefully kept apart. "the auditing organization notified the MDSAP regulators, and that notification went out within 5 business days. Health Canada then requested a corrective action plan, and the notified body asked for a 24-month retrospective review of the German site's complaints." Both phrases refer to the same body two sentences apart. Slides 6 and 20 consistently use "auditing organization" for MDSAP and "notified body" for MDR, and Case 2 (slide 25) correctly uses "notified body" because that case is an MDR audit.
findings.fix: Change the second reference to "the auditing organization also asked for a 24-month retrospective review".

findings.problem: Adjacent slides use "four" for two different things with nothing to distinguish them aloud. Slide 30: "One process, local annexes, governed interfaces, and audit-ready every day is the whole of this section in a single line, and the distance between a company that has all four and a company that has three of them is usually visible inside the first hour." Slide 31 then opens "these four tiers are how that decision gets written down". A listener carrying "all four" from the previous sentence will map it onto the four tiers.
findings.fix: On slide 31 say "the four tiers on this slide", and on slide 30 name them as principles: "a company with all four of those principles."

findings.problem: The Tuesday-at-08:10 scenario is used as a hypothetical and then reused verbatim as the real Case 1, so the two become indistinguishable. Slide 14: "It is 08:10 on a Tuesday morning, and 2 people you have never met are standing at your reception desk holding their credentials." Slide 15: "whoever is sitting at reception at 08:10 on a Tuesday is part of your quality system." Slide 22: "Two notified body auditors presented their credentials at reception at 08:10." The motif recurs on slide 35 ("than most manufacturers are in on a Tuesday morning") and slide 36 ("a humbling Tuesday you chose costs far less than the Tuesday your notified body chooses"). Slides 37 and 40 then switch to a different time for the same scenario: "auditors arrive tomorrow at 08:00" and "if they knocked tomorrow at 08:00".
findings.fix: Change the slide 14 hypothetical to a different time and day (e.g. "07:50 on a Thursday") so Case 1's 08:10 Tuesday reads as a real specific, and make slides 37 and 40 use the same time as slide 14 rather than a third one.

findings.problem: Three framings are each used three or more times across the deck. The "this is free" point: slide 16 "A laminated script at the front desk is the cheapest readiness investment you will ever make"; slide 35 "those 2 items cost nothing, they need no capital request"; slide 37 "not one of them requires a budget approval before you can start". The harmonize line, verbatim twice: slide 29 "harmonize the process, localize the annex, and govern the interfaces" and slide 37 "Harmonize the process, localize the annex, and govern the interfaces", plus slide 30's variant. And reception-as-QMS: slide 15 "whoever is sitting at reception at 08:10 on a Tuesday is part of your quality system" and slide 37 "because reception is part of your Quality Management System". The presenter's own voice also repeats: "I will always caution manufacturers" on slides 11, 18 and 34.
findings.fix: Keep the harmonize line only twice, once as Case 4's lesson (slide 29) and once as the takeaway (slide 37), and cut slide 30's variant. Keep one "costs nothing" statement, at slide 35 where it drives the Monday action. Vary the three "I will always caution manufacturers" openings.

findings.problem: Numerals and number-words are mixed inconsistently by chunk, which forces the presenter to make reading decisions mid-sentence. Slide 3 has "3 questions" while slides 22, 24, 26 and 28 all have "three questions". Slide 28 mixes both within eight lines: "Three good sites, three honest procedures", then "All 3 sites sit under a single ... certificate", then "there were 3 versions of the complaint form". Elsewhere: "Two threads run through" (slide 9) against "There are 2 I want to stress" (slide 18); "Two failures recur" (slide 10) against "the 2 companies now run" (slide 25); "Four deviations had been closed" (slide 25) against "4 case studies" (slide 1). Slide 34's "0 procedures" and "0 pieces of equipment" must be spoken as "zero" and are not written that way anywhere.
findings.fix: Spell out every number under ten as a word throughout, keep numerals only for clause numbers, dates, times and quantities over ten, and write "zero" wherever slide 34 has "0".

findings.problem: Em-dash asides and slide-furniture references assume the listener can see the page. Slide 11: "the installation qualification, the operational qualification, and the performance qualification - the IQ, OQ and PQ - for the process being observed that day", a 52-word sentence with a parenthetical the listener hears as a non-sequitur. Slide-furniture references are also phrased three different ways for the same element: "The transferable lesson sits on the band at the bottom" (slide 23), "As the band at the bottom has it" (slide 27), "The lesson on the band is" (slide 29), plus "You will note in the What Happened column" (slide 26), which names an on-slide label the audience may not be able to read.
findings.fix: On slide 11 split the aside into its own sentence: "...the installation, operational and performance qualifications. IQ, OQ and PQ." Standardise the band references to one phrase, and on slide 26 replace "the What Happened column" with "what the investigator found".

findings.problem: Two smaller items on slide 6. The count is wrong for what follows: "there are 6 regimes I want you to carry in your head", but the six headings include "ISO 13485 Itself", which is a standard rather than a regime, and "Other Major Markets", which bundles six separate national regimes (Brazil, Japan, China, Korea, Saudi Arabia, India). And "Saudi Arabia under the SFDA requirements" collides aurally with FDA, which the deck uses heavily; a listener hears "the FDA requirements". The date format also shifts: slide 5 has "since 2 Feb 2026" while slide 6 has "On 2 February 2026".
findings.fix: Say "six blocks of regulation" rather than "6 regimes". Say "the Saudi FDA, the SFDA" on first mention so the distinction is audible. Write every date out in full, as slide 6 does.

findings.problem: The same stock transition sentence opens ten slides, and it is the single loudest seam signature in the deck: "So now that we have established the sequence of events, we can begin to look at..." (6), "So now that we have established which definitions govern, we can begin to look at..." (8), "So now that we have a baseline understanding of what changed and what did not, we can move on to..." (11), "So now that we have established which 4 provisions carry the FDA-specific weight, we can begin to look at..." (12), "So now that we have a baseline understanding of the records content, we can move on to..." (14), "So now that we have established what the regulation says, we can begin to look at how it is inspected" (17), "So now that we have a baseline understanding of how a QMSR inspection actually runs, we can move on to..." (26), "So now that we have established what a crosswalk can and cannot do for you, we can begin to look at..." (27), "So now that we have established what the 2026 gap assessments keep finding, we can move on to..." (33), "So now that we have established the 5 phases and the 2 tracks, we can put dates against..." (38). Heard aloud in a 90-minute session this becomes a verbal tic that tells the audience a template is being filled in.
findings.fix: Keep the formula at most twice, at the two genuine act breaks (slide 17 into inspection, slide 26 into gap assessment). Rewrite the other eight as content-specific bridges that carry an idea rather than a structural announcement, e.g. slide 12: "Start with the hooks, because 820.10(b) is where the standard's phrase 'applicable regulatory requirements' gets its FDA-specific meaning." Slide 14: "Labeling is the one production control FDA wrote out in full, and this is why."

findings.problem: Seam after slide 21. Slide 22 opens as if the inspection section is only now beginning: "In order to understand how much the inspection itself has changed, we have to start with the records that used to sit outside of it." But the inspection section opened at slide 17 ("we can begin to look at how it is inspected") and slides 18 through 21 have already covered QSIT's withdrawal, the 6 QMS Areas, the two models, and the investigator's walk-through. Slide 22 also re-reveals FAQ 8 as news ("Some of you may be asking whether FDA can really call for your management review minutes now? FDA answered that in Frequently Asked Question number 8, and I am going to read it word for word, because it is unambiguous") when the same FAQ has already been used on slide 3, slide 8 and slide 10.
findings.fix: Rewrite the slide 22 opener to continue rather than restart, and drop the reveal framing: "We have said three times this morning that the 820.180(c) shield is gone. This slide is where I show you the exact words, because you will want to quote them back to your own leadership." Then read the FAQ 8 quote once, here, and cut the paraphrases from slides 3 and 8 (see separate finding).

findings.problem: FAQ number 8 / the loss of the 820.180(c) exemption is introduced as new information four separate times. Slide 3: "the old 21 CFR 820.180(c) 'shield' over management review, internal audit, and supplier audit records is gone. FDA's own frequently asked questions page indicates that these records should be readily available upon inspection, which is the single biggest behavioral change in the QMSR." Slide 8: "That exemption is gone, which FDA addressed in Comment 55, and FDA's FAQ number 8 says plainly that the agency has authority to inspect those records." Slide 10 Statement 2: "FAQ number 8 confirms that the 820.180(c) exceptions are not maintained, and that those records should be readily available upon inspection." Slide 22: the full verbatim quote. Each instance also claims or implies primacy ("the single biggest behavioral change").
findings.fix: Assign one job per instance. Slide 3 keeps the 15-minute test question but stops at "those records are now inspectable, and we will read FDA's exact words later this morning." Slide 8 becomes a one-line row in the disappeared-and-where-it-went list, cross-referencing without arguing. Slide 10 Statement 2 keeps the myth-or-fact call but answers in one line with no citation recap. Slide 22 is the only place the quote is read and the only place the phrase "single biggest behavioral change" appears.

findings.problem: Seam after slide 6. The deletion of proposed 820.15 is told twice, both times as a discovery. Slide 6: "Some of you may be asking what happened to 820.15? There is no 820.15. The proposed rule carried a 'Clarification of concepts' section at that number, FDA deleted it, and the clarifications moved into 820.3(b)". Slide 7: "The proposed 820.15, 'Clarification of concepts', was deleted, and its content was moved into 820.3(b)." Slide 4 had also promised it as a punchline ("a surprising amount of what circulates about the QMSR is wrong, and that includes a section number which does not exist"), so the audience gets the same reveal three slides running.
findings.fix: Keep the full telling on slide 6, where the punchline promised on slide 4 lands, including the consultant-crosswalk warning. On slide 7 cut the sentence entirely and open the dropped-definitions paragraph at "The proposed definitions for customer, design validation, nonconformity...", since slide 7's real subject is the four-layer hierarchy, not the deletion.

findings.problem: Seam after slide 26. Slide 26 exists only to make one point, and slide 27 makes it again with a fuller citation. Slide 26: "FDA declined to publish a crosswalk between the QS regulation and the QMSR, and in Comment 18 the agency explained that a one-to-one comparison would be cumbersome and not useful." Slide 27: "FDA declined to publish a clause-level crosswalk, which the agency addressed in Comment 18 of the final rule, so every clause-level crosswalk in circulation, this one included, is industry-authored." Two consecutive slides open with "FDA declined to publish a crosswalk... Comment 18."
findings.fix: Slide 26 should keep only the thesis it is actually for: "A crosswalk is where you start. It is not where you finish. Here is why that distinction decides your first 90 days." Move the Comment 18 fact and the industry-authored caveat wholly into slide 27, where the table is on screen and the provenance warning is load-bearing.

findings.problem: The recurring-deficiencies list is delivered near-verbatim on three slides. Slide 21: "The recurring deficiencies named at MedCon include: procedures that regurgitate the standard without stating what the firm actually does, vague or missing risk controls, inconsistent scoring across departments, hazard and harm used interchangeably, and risk analyses that were never updated with postmarket data." Slide 24: "procedures that 'regurgitate the regulation or the standard' and never say what is done or when, risk controls that are vague, missing, or hard to interpret, hazards confused with harms, risk scoring that is inconsistent between departments, risk analyses that are never updated with complaints, Medical Device Reports, or recalls". Slide 31 then delivers the same material a third time regrouped by QMS Area ("risk management confined to design while production, purchasing, and complaints never reference the risk file", "internal audits still running on Part 820 checklists").
findings.fix: Cut the list from slide 21 entirely and end that slide on the three-part risk answer, which is its real payload. Keep slide 24 as the enforcement-data slide, with the FDA-official quotes and the FY2025 baseline numbers, and cite the deficiency themes in one sentence rather than five. Slide 31 then earns its place as the only itemised list, because it is the one grouped by compliance program area and attributed finding by finding.

findings.problem: A promise made to the room in the opening poll is never kept. Slide 3: "Has your firm hosted an FDA inspection, or received a records request, since 2 February 2026? ... If that is you, I will come back to you during the inspection section, because what the investigator asked for first is the most useful piece of information in this room." Nothing in slides 17 through 24 comes back to those hands. There is no bracketed cue, no question to the room, and no reference to "what the investigator asked you for first" anywhere in the inspection section.
findings.fix: Add a resumption on slide 21, where pre-arrival review and the investigator's first ask are the subject, with a matching cue on its own line: "[GO BACK TO THE HANDS FROM THE OPENING POLL. ASK ONE OR TWO FIRMS WHAT THE INVESTIGATOR ASKED FOR FIRST, 60 SECONDS EACH]" followed by a line that ties whatever they say back to "that documentation is what selects the elements." If there is no room in the timing, delete the promise from slide 3.

findings.problem: An exercise is set up and never resumed. Slide 31: "Read down the 3 columns and mark the 3 findings you recognise... [PAUSE WHILE TABLES MARK THEIR THREE] Keep those 3 marks in front of you, because the next thing we do is put them under time pressure." Slide 32 then hands out a completely different set of material: "In your Exercise Pack you will find Exercise B, which is 8 gap cards and a one-page triage grid, and every one of those 8 cards is drawn from a real 2026 finding rather than written to make a point." The marked three are never scored, never sorted, never mentioned again; Exercise C on slide 38 draws instead on "what you saw in Exercise A and Exercise B."
findings.fix: Pick one. Either have Exercise B score the participants' own three marks alongside the 8 cards ("score your own three on the same grid, and see where they land against the cards"), and reference them again on slide 38; or cut the slide 31 marking activity and its bracketed cue and end slide 31 on "This is by no means an exhaustive list," letting slide 32 open the exercise cleanly.

findings.problem: The close does not land the promise the opening made. Slide 3 builds the whole session around a named test: "The third question is the one the rest of the session is built around, and I will call it the 15-minute test. Could you hand an investigator your last 2 management reviews and this year's internal audit reports within 15 minutes..." Fifteen minutes is then the standard on slide 34 ("a median retrieval time under 15 minutes") and slide 36 ("a median time to produce a requested record of 15 minutes or less"). But slide 41 closes on a different question with a different number: "could your people walk them to a complaint, a change, a supplier control, and a management review decision in 10 minutes?" The listener who has been carrying the 15-minute test for 90 minutes hears the number change at the exact moment the deck should be closing the loop.
findings.fix: Close on the opening test, restated: "I opened with the 15-minute test. Here it is again, with the thread attached: if an investigator opened your risk file tomorrow and picked one high-severity hazard, could your people walk them from that hazard to a complaint, a change, a supplier control, and a management review decision, and could they do it in the same 15 minutes?" That keeps one number for the whole deck and makes the close an answer rather than a new question.

findings.problem: Q&A is opened twice, and the deck ends on generic boilerplate that reads as a different speaker. The slide first opens the floor properly ("I am happy to take questions on anything we covered today, and the areas that tend to come up include..."), then adds a second, stock ending that opens it again: "So with that said, it is easy to recognize why the evidence, and not the vocabulary, is what decides how these inspections go for manufacturers working through this transition. This concludes the presentation portion of this discussion. I want to thank each of you who attended, and I welcome any questions you may have at this time." "This concludes the presentation portion of this discussion" is filler, and "it is easy to recognize why" tells the audience their conclusion instead of earning it.
findings.fix: Delete the final paragraph entirely. End on the thank-you and the materials: "...and I am glad to take follow-up questions by email once you are back at your site. Evidence, not vocabulary. That is the whole session in three words. Thank you." One close, one floor-opening, one last line.

findings.problem: "OAFRs" is used as a bare acronym ten slides before it is expanded, and the inspection framework is pre-empted. Slide 8: "is replaced by Compliance Program 7382.850, which brings 6 QMS Areas, 4 OAFRs, and 2 inspection models." The expansion does not arrive until slide 18: "replaced by 6 QMS Areas and 4 Other Applicable FDA Requirements, or OAFRs." A listener hearing "four oh-a-eff-arrs" on slide 8 has nothing to attach it to, and slide 18's "There are 2 structural changes here" is no longer news.
findings.fix: On slide 8 replace the acronym string with a forward pointer in plain words: "...is replaced by Compliance Program 7382.850, which we will spend fifteen minutes on after the break, because it is the single largest change in this transition." Leave the expansion, the six areas and the two models to slide 18, which is built for them.

findings.problem: A stated count does not match what is delivered, and the audience is invited to count along. Slide 28: "The second half of the crosswalk carries the rows where the old FDA language has genuinely gone away, and there are 3 of them I want to point out." Four rows are then discussed at length: process validation ("Old 820.75 maps to 7.5.6"), nonconforming product and rework ("Nonconforming product moves to 8.3.1 through 8.3.4"), complaint files ("Complaint files under 820.198 now map to 3 clauses rather than 1"), and the records row ("Then there is the row that matters most for this session, which is the records row").
findings.fix: Either say four, or demote one. Cleanest: "there are 4 of them I want to point out," since the records row is explicitly flagged as the one that matters most for this session and cannot be cut.

findings.problem: "There are 7 dates that matter, and I want to walk them in order" is followed by at least twelve dates: 23 February 2022, 24 May 2022, 2 February 2024, 31 January 2024, 15 October 2024, 4 December 2025, 16 December 2025, 14 January 2026, 1 April 2026, 2 February 2026, 27 May 2026, 21 July 2026, 24 July 2026. The slide also stacks three provenance caveats inside those dates ("the public-inspection date rather than the publication date"; "the compliance program's own cover page says issued 2 February 2026, while law firms reported it posted on 30 January, and either way it applied from day one"), which stalls the opening six minutes in footnotes.
findings.fix: Say "There are seven moments that matter" and group explicitly to seven: proposal, final rule, the batch-or-lot correction, the technical amendments, FDA's explaining winter, the effective date, and the first Warning Letters. Move both source caveats to the handout and to slide 37, where "anything in your handout marked 'reported' comes from secondary sources" already lives.

findings.problem: Track A is internally contradictory, at the slide where half the room is being told what to do. "Track A is the firms that have finished the transition, and those firms enter at Phase 4 now." The instructions that follow are Phase 0, 1, 2 and 3 work: "Confirm your process owners" (Phase 0 exit criterion), "re-run the assessment on the high-exposure rows only" (Phase 1), "confirm that your templates actually carry the 820.35 and 820.45 elements" (Phase 2), "refresh training for your front-room staff" (Phase 3), and only then "run the mock inspection" (Phase 4). A listener who wrote down "enter at Phase 4" now hears four phases of work.
findings.fix: Say what is actually meant: "Track A firms are aiming at Phase 4, and they get there by running Phases 0 through 3 in compressed form, on the high-exposure rows only." Then keep the list as is, labelling each item with its phase so the audience can follow.

findings.problem: The Track B week plan does not match the phases it claims to compress. "Track B is the firms still closing gaps, and the week numbers in the last column compress Phases 1 through 4 into 90 days: week 1 to mobilize, weeks 1 through 3 to assess, weeks 3 through 5 to design, weeks 5 through 9 to implement and train, weeks 9 through 13 to verify, and sustain from week 13 onward." Mobilize is Phase 0 and sustain is Phase 5, so the plan actually compresses Phases 0 through 5, not 1 through 4.
findings.fix: "...the week numbers in the last column compress Phase 0 through Phase 4 into 90 days, with Sustain starting at week 13." Same list, correct label, and the audience's notes will match the workbook.

findings.problem: Participants are sent to a facilitator-only document. Slide 25: "The model observations are in your Facilitator Guide, and you'll notice they all do the same thing..." But slide 1 tells the room there are exactly three participant materials: "the Participant Handout... the Workshop Exercise Pack... and the Gap Assessment Workbook." Slide 32 then uses a fourth, vaguer name for the same kind of content: "the reasoning on both of them is written up in the session materials in your pack."
findings.fix: Use the three names from slide 1 and nothing else. Slide 25: "The model observations are in the Workshop Exercise Pack, at the back of Exercise A." Slide 32: "The reasoning on both of those cards is in the Workshop Exercise Pack, behind the Exercise B grid." Slide 41's "all linked below" should also say which three.

findings.problem: Slide 23 is one unbroken block of prose with no paragraph breaks, and it contains sentences no speaker can deliver in one breath. The worst is roughly 75 words: "The citation now reads 'as required by ISO 13485:2016, Clause 7.1', and the firm's own procedure is quoted back at it by document number, in this case a risk management procedure, TM-112, which does not define how risk management activities are performed and documented, who is responsible for conducting and approving them, when the documentation must be updated, or how post-market feedback data including complaints, adverse events, and recalls is incorporated." A second runs about 55 words: "Both letters open with the same sentence, which is that the devices are adulterated under section 501(h)..."
findings.fix: Break the slide into four short paragraphs, one per idea: what the format is, the risk-management example, the supplier-controls example, and what to do about it. Split the TM-112 sentence into three: "The firm's own procedure is quoted back at it by document number. In this case, a risk management procedure, TM-112. FDA lists four things it failed to define: how risk activities are performed, who approves them, when they are updated, and how post-market feedback comes in."

findings.problem: Two clause strings are unspeakable as written, and the second is a bare list of ten numbers with no anchors. Slide 15: "the clauses named include: Clause 4.1, Clause 5 and its subclauses, and 6.1, together with 820.10, Clause 7.3 and its subclauses, Clause 7.4 and its subclauses, Clause 8.2.2 together with 820.35(a), Clauses 8.4 and 8.5, Clause 7.5.3, and Clause 7.5.4 together with 820.35(b)." Slide 35 repeats it worse: "specifically 4.1, 5, 6.1, 7.3, 7.4, 8.2.2, 8.4, 8.5, 7.5.3, and 7.5.4." Read aloud, both are pure noise; the listener cannot hold ten clause numbers and has no idea what any of them govern.
findings.fix: Name the subject, not the number, and send the numbers to the handout. Slide 15: "4.4(b)(1) now calls up ISO clauses instead of QSR sections, and they cover the quality system itself, management responsibility, resources, design, purchasing, complaint handling, analysis of data, improvement, production, and servicing. The clause numbers for each are in the handout at section 5." Slide 35 should then say "the ten clauses called up by 4.4(b)(1), with evidence behind each one" and stop.

findings.problem: The back fifteen minutes carries nine slides, several of them dense, plus a solo exercise and a commitment round from every table. Slide 2 promises: "the last 15 minutes cover the roadmap, the metrics that belong in management review, and your own 90-day plan." What actually sits there is slides 33, 34 (five phases and two tracks, the densest table in the deck), 35 (three archetypes with full requirement lists), 36 (twelve metrics in three groups), 37 (watch list and resources, which slide 2 never mentions), 38 (Exercise C: three minutes solo plus "[TAKE ONE COMMITMENT FROM EACH TABLE BEFORE ADVANCING]"), 39 (five takeaways "I want to go through them slowly"), 40 (references), 41 (Q&A). Exercise C alone, with a commitment from every table, is four to six minutes.
findings.fix: Re-time slide 2 to name the real shape, and cut for it: fold slide 35's archetypes into the handout and refer to them in two sentences, cut slide 37 to a single line pointing at the handout's resource page, and drop slide 40 to "the full list is in your handout, with live links." That buys roughly six minutes for Exercise C and the five takeaways, which are the slides that have to land.

findings.problem: Exercise A cannot be done in the time given. "For the next 6 minutes your table is not the manufacturer" then asks for: three questions plus one element to dig into; a written observation naming clause, record and failure; a sheet swap with the next table; and a five-part response skeleton ("the correction, the root cause, the systemic action, the evidence date, and the effectiveness metric") for a stranger's observation. That is three distinct deliverables plus a hand-off, against three source documents the table has to read first. Exercise B on slide 32 has the same problem: score 8 cards on 3 dimensions, sort them, pick a top 3 with an owner role and a 30-day action each, and "let the argument run for a minute" on two deliberately arguable cards, all in "6 minutes on the clock once I stop talking."
findings.fix: Either extend both to 10 minutes and take the time from slides 35, 37 and 40, or cut scope. For A, drop the three-questions step and run read, observation, swap, response. For B, pre-score four of the eight cards on the handout so tables score only four, and make the two arguable cards the explicit centre of the exercise rather than an add-on.

findings.problem: Acronyms are expanded repeatedly, chunk by chunk, which is the clearest fingerprint of separate writers. QSIT three times (slides 1, 8, 18: "the Quality System Inspection Technique, or QSIT"). MDSAP four times (9, 15, 35, 37: "the Medical Device Single Audit Program, or MDSAP"). UDI five times (6, 12, 19, 24, 35). CGMP twice (9, 15). QMS twice in consecutive slides (6, 7: "a quality management system, or QMS"). OAFRs twice (18, 36). DHF twice (8, 32). PMA twice (8, 34), with bare "PMA" used on slides 9, 18, 19 and 20 in between. QMSR twice (1, 37).
findings.fix: Expand each acronym exactly once, at first use, and keep a single expansion register: QMSR and QSIT on slide 1, QMS and UDI on slide 6, MDSAP and CGMP and PMA on slide 9, DHF on slide 8, OAFR on slide 18. Every later use is bare. Where a late slide genuinely needs a reminder, use a half-line ("the six QMS Areas, from slide 19") rather than a full re-expansion.

findings.problem: Two acronyms are used before they are ever expanded. Slide 28 says "820.10(b)(3) adds the MDR evaluation hook"; MDR is not expanded until slide 35 ("Medical Device Reporting, or MDR"). Slide 21 says "your GUDID entries" with no expansion anywhere before it; slide 12 had written it out in full without the acronym ("your Global Unique Device Identification Database records") and slide 38 writes it out in full again.
findings.fix: On slide 28 write "the Medical Device Reporting evaluation hook" in full, and attach the acronym at slide 12 where the database is first named: "your Global Unique Device Identification Database, or GUDID, records." Then slides 21 and 38 can both use GUDID bare.

findings.problem: OAI is used before it is expanded, across a chunk seam. Slide 21: "changes which appear to require a new 510(k) or a new PMA also trigger an OAI recommendation." Slide 22 then expands it as if new: "among its examples of an Official Action Indicated, or OAI, outcome."
findings.fix: Expand on slide 21, where Situation 1 is introduced and the phrase "Official Action Indicated examples" already appears: "...the Official Action Indicated, or OAI, examples." Slide 22 then uses OAI bare.

findings.problem: The agenda is delivered twice in the first two slides. Slide 1: "We will discuss what actually changed on 2 February 2026 and... what did not change. We will also identify the 4 FDA-specific provisions... We will explore how the inspection process itself now works... We will delve into an exposure-weighted method for gap assessment... Finally, we will discuss a phased roadmap with exit criteria." Slide 2 walks the identical five blocks with minute counts: "We spend the first 6 minutes on welcome, objectives, and a short room poll. From there we take roughly 14 minutes on what changed... then 10 minutes on the 4 load-bearing FDA-specific provisions... 15 minutes on the inspection itself..."
findings.fix: Cut the five "we will" sentences from slide 1 to a single promise: "By the end of the ninety minutes you will have an exposure-ranked gap list and the first ninety days of a roadmap, written in your own hand." Let slide 2 carry the structure, which is what it is for.

findings.problem: Three pieces of guidance are given twice, once in the first half of the deck and again on slide 22. (1) Confidentiality marking, slide 13: "Mark them in advance of the inspection, and never redact what you hand over. A confidentiality marking isn't a shield against review." Slide 22: "do not redact what you hand over. Mark the records that are genuinely confidential under section 820.35(d) before the inspection rather than in the middle of it." (2) Notified body audits, slide 9: "FDA added that a notified body audit does not replace your own internal audit under Clause 8.2.4, which catches firms who assumed the 2 could be merged." Slide 22: "an ISO 13485 audit performed by your notified body does not replace your own internal audit under Clause 8.2.4." (3) Pre-2026 records, slide 9: "Records created before 2 February 2026 are 'fair game' if the inspection leads there." Slide 22: pre-2026 records "are still fair game for us to look at if the inspection direction leads us there."
findings.fix: Keep each once, where it is most useful. Confidentiality marking belongs on slide 22 with the other hand-over behaviour, so cut the two sentences from slide 13. The notified body point belongs on slide 9 in the what-did-not-change column, so cut it from slide 22. "Fair game" belongs on slide 22 as the Keisha Thomas quote, so slide 9 should say only "pre-2026 records remain inspectable" without the phrase.

findings.problem: The exposure definition is read out twice on consecutive slides, the second time as if it were new. Slide 30: "how exposed the requirement is, which means asking whether an investigator would read this record on day one, whether it sits in Model 2's minimum list, and whether it is one of the top-cited areas." Slide 32: "The exposure column is the one that does the real work... so I will read the definitions into the room. Exposure is high when an investigator reads that record on day one, when it sits in Model 2's minimum list, or when it is a top-5 cited area."
findings.fix: Slide 32 should reference rather than redefine: "Exposure is the column that does the real work, and it is the one tables argue about. Same three tests I gave you on the last slide: day one, Model 2's minimum list, top five cited. What is new here is medium and low." Then define only medium and low.

findings.problem: Hedge and disclaimer formulas are used about twenty times, which flattens the ones that matter. "It is important to note that" or "It should be noted that" or "It is important to remember that" appears on slides 5, 9, 13, 14, 15, 19, 21, 22, 24, 27 (twice), 34, 35 and 37. Six near-identical scope disclaimers also appear: "this is a general description" (14), "these are 3 common arrangements and not a complete map" (15), "This is by no means an exhaustive map" (19), "treat this as a general picture rather than a prediction" (20), "this is a general mapping" (27), "This is by no means an exhaustive list" (31), "these are archetypes rather than categories" (35). "I always recommend" appears on 23, 29 and 38; "I will always caution that" on 6 and 20.
findings.fix: Keep at most four disclaimers, at the four places a listener could actually over-generalise: slide 15 (Part 4 and contract roles), slide 20 (which inspection type you draw), slide 27 (the crosswalk's provenance) and slide 31 (the composite findings list). Delete the rest, and replace "It is important to note that" with the sentence's own subject: "Automated readers are allowed, with human oversight" rather than "It is important to note that FDA allows..."

findings.problem: Two different section counts for the same technical amendments will sound like a contradiction to anyone tracking numbers. Slide 5: "the technical amendments published at 90 FR 55978, and those re-pointed 179 sections across 18 CFR parts." Slide 15: "the technical amendments of December 2025 re-pointed 162 classification regulations to 820.35." Both may be true (total sections versus classification regulations specifically), but nothing in the text says so.
findings.fix: Make the relationship explicit at the second mention. Slide 15: "the December 2025 technical amendments re-pointed 179 sections in all, and 162 of those were Class I classification regulations pointed at 820.35."

findings.problem: A run of bare statistics is unspeakable and unmemorable: "FDA's own 483 data for FY2025 records 791 system-generated device 483s, with top citations of corrective and preventive action procedures, or CAPA, under 820.100(a) at 279, complaint procedures under 820.198(a) at 211, purchasing controls at 115, nonconforming product at 95, and process validation at 93." Spoken, that is six numbers and two CFR citations in one sentence, and "483s" as a plural is awkward aloud.
findings.fix: Give the shape, not the table: "For a baseline: FDA wrote about eight hundred device Form 483s in FY2025. CAPA procedures led, cited roughly two hundred and eighty times. Complaint procedures were second, at about two hundred. Purchasing, nonconforming product and process validation followed. The exact figures and citations are in your handout." The point, which the slide then makes, is that the ranking barely moved.

findings.problem: Numbers tangle into a tongue-twister at the one place the deck says the online crosswalks get it wrong: "So Model 2 is 22 or 23 elements plus 4 OAFRs, or it is 22 or 23 plus none, depending on which of those 2 uses you drew." The citation immediately before it is also hard to say and impossible to hear: "because Part III.D.1 through 4 each say to evaluate during all risk-based inspections except PMA preapproval, and Part III.C tells the investigator to exclude the OAFR elements where the subject device is not yet on the US market."
findings.fix: Split and name the two cases: "So: baseline surveillance is the minimum list plus the four OAFRs. PMA preapproval is the minimum list alone, because the device is not on the market yet. Same model, two different answers. The paragraph references are on the slide." Drop the spoken Part III citations.

findings.problem: Two citations are effectively unsayable and, heard aloud, meaningless. Slide 10 Statement 5: "Compliance Program 7382.850 at Part III.1.B(3) provides that records are selected on identified product risk and on investigator judgment." Slide 10 Statement 6: "risk management throughout the QMS is required through ISO 13485 at Clauses 4.1, 7.1, 7.3, 7.4, 7.5, 7.6, and 8.2" is seven clause numbers in a row in a rapid-fire round.
findings.fix: In a myth-or-fact round the answer should be one spoken line with the citation on the slide only. Statement 5: "Myth. Record selection is product risk plus investigator judgment. There are no sampling tables, and the paragraph reference is on the screen." Statement 6: "Myth, with a caveat. 14971 is not incorporated. But risk management is threaded through seven clauses of 13485, listed on the slide, and telling an investigator that 14971 is not mandatory has not gone well for anyone."

findings.problem: Slide 40 is two roughly 70-word citation sentences read aloud, and it is built around left and right positions the listener cannot see: "On the left is the regulation and the rulemaking history, which includes Part 820 as in force from 2 February 2026 on the eCFR, the final rule at 89 FR 7496 together with the correction at 89 FR 82945, the proposed rule at 87 FR 10119, the technical amendments at 90 FR 55978, 21 CFR 4.4 for combination products along with Parts 803, 806, 821, 830, and Part 11, and then ISO 13485:2016 and Clause 3 of ISO 9000:2015." The slide itself says copying is unnecessary, which makes reading the list aloud self-defeating.
findings.fix: Say the two categories and stop: "Two columns here. Regulation and rulemaking history on one side, FDA's own implementation and enforcement material on the other. Every item is in your handout with a live link, so I am not going to read Federal Register citations at you. If you only open three things: the final rule preamble, the compliance program's Attachment A, and the three Warning Letters."

findings.problem: Bracketed cues are inconsistent between chunks in ways a facilitator reading live will trip on. Number style varies: "[TAKE ONE OBSERVATION AND THE MATCHING RESPONSE FROM EACH OF 2 TABLES, 90 SECONDS EACH]" (25) against "[TAKE THE TOP THREE AND THE FIRST ACTION FROM TWO TABLES, 90 SECONDS EACH]" (32) and "[PAUSE WHILE TABLES MARK THEIR THREE]" (31). Terminal punctuation varies: "[VOTE ON EACH RECORD IN TURN. 10 SECONDS, THEN REVEAL.]" and "[TABLE WORK - 6 MINUTES. CIRCULATE.]" carry stops, while "[PAUSE FOR SHOW OF HANDS]" and "[TAKE ONE COMMITMENT FROM EACH TABLE BEFORE ADVANCING]" do not.
findings.fix: Pick one house style and apply it to all eleven cues: capitals, digits for numbers, no terminal period, em dash for duration. So "[TAKE TOP 3 AND FIRST ACTION FROM 2 TABLES — 90 SECONDS EACH]", "[TABLE WORK — 6 MINUTES, CIRCULATE]", "[PAUSE WHILE TABLES MARK THEIR 3]".

findings.problem: An action the facilitator physically performs is buried in spoken text instead of a cue, so a presenter reading aloud will say it rather than do it: "I am writing rough counts on the flipchart, and the reason is that a room full of firms who are complete and verified wants Track A of the roadmap..." Every other physical action in the deck is bracketed.
findings.fix: Split it: add "[WRITE ROUGH COUNTS ON FLIPCHART]" on its own line after the first [PAUSE FOR SHOW OF HANDS], then speak only the reason: "I am keeping rough counts, because a room that is complete and verified wants Track A, and a room still closing gaps wants Track B."

findings.problem: Three report-back cues duplicate instructions that were just spoken, so the instruction is delivered twice in a row. Slide 25: "Let us bring it back together and hear from 2 tables, 90 seconds each. Give me the observation first, in the clause, record, failure form..." immediately followed by "[TAKE ONE OBSERVATION AND THE MATCHING RESPONSE FROM EACH OF 2 TABLES, 90 SECONDS EACH]". Same pattern on slide 32 ("I would like 2 tables to give me their top 3... I will hold you to about 90 seconds" then the cue) and slide 38 ("So, one sentence from each table, and start the sentence with a date and the words 'we will'" then the cue).
findings.fix: Keep the spoken line as the instruction to the room, and shorten each cue to the facilitator's own action: "[TAKE 2 — HOLD TO 90 SECONDS EACH]", "[TAKE 2 — 90 SECONDS EACH]", "[GO ROUND EVERY TABLE BEFORE ADVANCING]". The audience hears it once; the facilitator sees the timing.

findings.problem: Slide titles are present in four chunks and absent in three, tracking the authorship boundaries exactly. Slides 7 through 16 carry titles ("Which Definition Wins", "What Disappeared, and Where It Went", "Spot Check on 5 Complaint Records"), as do 22 through 26 and 32 through 41. Slides 1 through 6, 17 through 21 and 27 through 31 have bare "SLIDE n" lines with no title. Register also splits along the same lines: British spellings appear only in the middle chunks ("servicing records must be analysed", slide 13; "service reports never analysed", slide 31; "the 3 findings you recognise", slide 31) against American elsewhere ("it is easy to recognize", slide 41). Contractions are mixed the same way: mostly "do not" and "does not", but "isn't" (13, 23), "don't" (14, 21, 25), "you'll" (25), "let's" (32), "doesn't" (30). Slide 1 also has a typo in the handoff line: "So with that said, lets dive in."
findings.fix: Add titles to slides 1 through 6, 17 through 21 and 27 through 31 in the same voice as the existing ones. Standardise on US spelling throughout (analyzed, recognize). Pick one contraction policy, and given the rest of the register, expand the six contractions to full forms. Fix "lets" to "let's".

findings.problem: "...and they include:" is used repeatedly to introduce lists that are complete, not partial, which is both wrong and a written colon the listener cannot hear. Slide 6: "The remaining sections are reserved, and they include: 820.5, 820.20 through 820.30, 820.40, and Subparts C through O" (that is all of them). Slide 1: "You have 3 companion materials with you today, and they include:" followed by all three. Slide 12: "The hooks in 820.10(b) include:" followed by all four. The same construction appears on slides 5, 7, 13, 14, 15, 21, 27, 31, 32, 34, 35, 36 and 41.
findings.fix: Use "are" for complete lists and "include" only for genuinely partial ones, and drop the spoken colon in favour of a countable lead-in: "Three companion materials: the Participant Handout, the Exercise Pack, and the Gap Assessment Workbook." "820.10(b) has four hooks. UDI assignment, product tracking, reporting to FDA, advisory notices."

findings.problem: The opening promises table work for the 90-day plan, but Exercise C is solo. Slide 1: "you will build the first 90 days of that roadmap at your own table before we finish." Slide 38 delivers: "there is one card for each participant. You will have 3 minutes on your own with that card" and "[SOLO WORK - 3 MINUTES. CIRCULATE.]". Slide 2 hedges differently again: "the last 15 minutes cover... your own 90-day plan."
findings.fix: Align all three on what actually happens: slide 1 "you will write the first 90 days of that roadmap yourself, on a card, before we finish"; slide 2 keeps "your own 90-day plan"; slide 38 unchanged. Slide 2's "The 3 table exercises" should then read "The 3 exercises."

findings.problem: "Situation 1" is used as known terminology twelve slides before it is explained. Slide 9: "The compliance-action threshold has not changed, and the Situation 1 examples were simply updated for the QMSR." It is not defined until slide 21: "Situation 1 of the compliance program, which holds the Official Action Indicated examples, was rewritten for the QMSR."
findings.fix: On slide 9 describe it instead of naming it: "The compliance-action threshold has not changed. FDA's own examples of what warrants action were rewritten into QMSR language, and we will read them in the inspection section." Keep the term and its definition together on slide 21.

findings.problem: The audience-voice question device is used four times with three different framings, and slide 30's version reads as though a participant actually spoke. Slide 6: "Some of you may be asking what happened to 820.15?" Slide 14: "So now you may be asking, how much of this can be automated?" Slide 20: "So now you may be asking, how do the OAFRs apply under Model 2?" Slide 30: "So you have given me the mapping, but how do I work out what my site fixes first?" Slide 22's version is also a statement punctuated as a question, which the listener cannot hear: "Some of you may be asking whether FDA can really call for your management review minutes now?"
findings.fix: Use one framing, and make every instance a real question. Slide 30: "So you may be asking: you have given me the mapping, but how do I work out what my site fixes first?" Slide 22: "Some of you are wondering whether FDA can really call for your management review minutes. Here is the answer, in FDA's words." Cap the device at three uses across the deck.

findings.problem: Two different fifteens sit close together and will be confused when heard rather than read. Slide 3 establishes "the 15-minute test" for record retrieval, reinforced on slides 34 and 36. Slide 23 then says "you will need to respond in the same vocabulary within 15 business days."
findings.fix: Disambiguate audibly on slide 23: "...and you will have fifteen business days, not fifteen minutes, to respond in that same vocabulary." The contrast makes the coincidence useful instead of confusing.

summary:
Needs work. The eight chunks are individually well-written and factually consistent (the UDI ranking, the 7 and 6 record-element counts, the Warning Letter dates and the FAQ numbering all agree across chunks), but they do not read as one person talking straight through, and the deck is over-scoped for 90 minutes.

The seams are unmistakable. A single stock transition sentence ("So now that we have established X, we can begin to look at Y") opens ten slides. Slide titles are present in four chunks and absent in three, exactly along authorship lines, and British spellings and contractions cluster the same way. Acronyms are re-expanded chunk by chunk: QSIT three times, MDSAP four, UDI five. Two acronyms run backwards, with "OAFRs" used bare on slide 8 and expanded on 18, and "MDR" used on 28 and expanded on 35.

Three seams are substantive rather than cosmetic. Slide 7 re-tells the deletion of proposed 820.15 that slide 6 has just revealed. Slides 26 and 27 both open with "FDA declined to publish a crosswalk... Comment 18." Worst, slide 22 restarts the inspection section six slides after it began ("we have to start with the records that used to sit outside of it") and re-reveals FAQ 8 as news when slides 3, 8 and 10 have already used it — the loss of the 820.180(c) shield is introduced as new information four separate times.

Two promises are broken. The opening poll on slide 3 tells inspected firms "I will come back to you during the inspection section"; nothing in slides 17 to 24 does. Slide 31 has tables mark three findings and "keep those 3 marks in front of you" for the next exercise; Exercise B then hands out eight unrelated gap cards and the marks are never used.

The close misses the opening. Slide 3 names "the 15-minute test" and builds the session on it; slide 41 closes on a 10-minute question instead, then opens Q&A twice and ends on boilerplate ("This concludes the presentation portion of this discussion").

On deliverability: three counts are wrong ("7 dates" followed by twelve, "3 of them" followed by four rows, Track B's "Phases 1 through 4" that actually spans Phase 0 to Phase 5), Track A is told to "enter at Phase 4" and then given four phases of work, both table exercises are scoped well past their six minutes, the back fifteen minutes carries nine slides, and slide 25 sends participants to a Facilitator Guide that is not one of the three materials they were given. Speakability fails hardest at slide 23 (one unbroken block containing a 75-word sentence), the ten-clause strings on slides 15 and 35, and the citation walls on slides 24 and 40.

findings.problem: Deck-wide antithesis saturation. "rather than" runs 26 times (2.0 per 1,000 words) against 3 times in the corpus (0.2 per 1,000) - a tenfold increase - and the bare "X, not Y" construction appears about 14 more times, a move the corpus makes essentially never. Samples: "a risk file is an argument, not an archive" (39); "The Order of Priority Is an Order, Not a Menu" (22); "A File, Not a Folder" (6); "it is a list rather than a suggestion" (32); "the notified body checks the joints rather than the pipes" (33); "it starts from the device rather than from the file" (30); "the file that is a folder rather than an argument" (5); "a documentation difference, not a difference of substance" (14); "is a finding, not a conclusion" (25); "you have renamed the problem rather than analysed it" (20). This is the single most pervasive tell in the draft and it is a generic-AI rhetorical reflex, not his.
findings.fix: Cut at least two thirds of these. He states the point positively and adds the contrast as a separate sentence if at all: not "it is a list rather than a suggestion" but "This is a required list. Manufacturers are required to collect from each of these sources." Not "A risk file is an argument, not an archive" but "It is important to note that the risk management file is required to carry the argument for each risk decision, and not simply to hold the records." Keep at most three or four of the sharpest contrasts across 39 slides.

findings.problem: Verbless fragments used for rhetorical emphasis. The corpus contains none - every short sentence in it is a complete instructional imperative ("Document these efforts thoroughly.", "Don't make this selection in isolation."). The draft has a dozen: "Not cost, not schedule, not manufacturability." (13, also a rhetorical triple, exactly the flagged AI register); "Shall, and in this order." (22); "Both of those, separately." (22); "Not significant residual risks - any." (22); "Not as law, in either jurisdiction." (39); "Read it." (18); "Then e)." and "And g)." (9); "You have a roll-up." (25); "That is the entire definition." (6).
findings.fix: Restore them to full sentences in his cadence. "Not cost, not schedule, not manufacturability." becomes "It is important to note that cost, schedule and manufacturability are not permitted limits under this provision." "Shall, and in this order." becomes "You will note that the regulation uses the word shall, and that it sets these options out in a fixed order." "Both of those, separately." becomes "It should be noted that both of those determinations are required, and they are required separately." "Read it." becomes "I would ask you to take a moment to read through the row before we go on."

findings.problem: Pronoun discipline is inverted against the corpus. "manufacturers/manufacturer" drops from 6.2 per 1,000 words in the corpus to 1.2 in the draft, while "you" rises from 5.0 to 12.8. In the corpus, regulatory obligation is attributed to manufacturers ("Manufacturers must accurately identify their device's classification", "manufacturers must submit clear, accurate, and complete labeling", "It is critical that manufacturers assess the risk") and second person is reserved for the audience's own artefacts ("your device", "your regulatory strategy"). The draft puts the regulator's requirements in second person throughout: "The sources you are required to collect from include" (32); "7.5 requires you to review every risk control measure" (7); "7.6 requires you to show that every identified hazardous situation has been considered" (7); "it asks you to confirm that the risks from all identified hazardous situations have been considered" (24); "you are required to evaluate the impact of information from production and from post-market surveillance" (33).
findings.fix: Move the obligation back onto manufacturers and keep "you/your" for the participant's own file. "The sources you are required to collect from include" becomes "Manufacturers are required to collect information from the following sources:". "7.5 requires you to review every risk control measure" becomes "Clause 7.5 requires manufacturers to review every risk control measure for new hazards and for effects on the existing estimates." "your file", "your procedure" and "your risk management plan" can stay as they are.

findings.problem: British spelling throughout, where the corpus is uniformly American. Draft: "a spreadsheet with a colour matrix" (2), "colour" again (29), "categorisation system" (6), "the minimisation requirement" (12), "are minimised" (13), "The generalisation out of Exercise B" (30), "labelling" and "labelled" (30, 38), "rather than analysed it" (20), "plasticiser-free set" (24), "Effectiveness is comprehension and behaviour" (23) plus "behaviour" twice more (8, 29), "engineering judgement" (29, 30) and "judgement" (13), four in total, "the conceptual centre of the section" (25), "recognised" (11). The corpus writes "labeling" 17 times, "behavior" twice, "minimize/minimizing/minimization", "recognize", "organized", "prioritizing", "standardized", "generalizability" - never a single British form.
findings.fix: Convert all of these to American forms: colour to color, categorisation to categorization, minimisation/minimised to minimization/minimized, generalisation to generalization, labelling/labelled to labeling/labeled, analysed to analyzed, plasticiser to plasticizer, behaviour to behavior, judgement to judgment, centre to center, recognised to recognized. "harmonised standard" may stay as the EU legal term of art, but make it the only exception and keep it consistent.

findings.problem: A colon-introduced list is run inline as prose, producing a construction found nowhere in the corpus. "The questions a reviewer arrives with are predictable, and the places the file has to answer them from include: Where did this hazard come from, which the file answers from 5.3 characteristics related to safety and 5.4 hazard identification. How did this hazard reach a harm, which is 5.4 again... Where did this number come from, which is 5.5 risk estimation..." Questions are capitalised, stripped of question marks, and restarted as fresh sentences after a colon. In the corpus every single "include:" / "This includes:" ends a line and is followed by a genuine bulleted or numbered list. The same inline-list workaround recurs on slides 5, 11, 13, 24, 25, 30 and 32 ("which include: the plan written too late, the chain collapsed into a single row...", "those clauses include: 4.1.2 b), 7.1, the design, purchasing...").
findings.fix: Break these back into the corpus list format - a lead-in sentence ending in a colon, then hyphen-bulleted or numbered items, exactly as in "Some general examples include:" or "The key requirements for any manufacturer to ensure a successful 510(k) submission include:". On slide 6: "The questions a reviewer arrives with are predictable, and the file has to be able to answer each of them:" followed by bullets such as "- Where did this hazard come from? This is answered from 5.3, characteristics related to safety, and 5.4, hazard identification."

findings.problem: Paragraph-level connective tissue has been swapped out for a different writer's. The draft contains zero instances of "Furthermore", "Additionally", "In addition", "Ultimately" and "This means" - which appear 6, 5, 2, 6 and 2 times respectively in the corpus and are his workhorse transitions - and only 3 of "However," against 11. In their place the draft uses "which means" 11 times and "In practice" 6 times, both of which are zero in the corpus, plus long comma-and chains: "ALARP is the familiar test, and it is familiar for understandable reasons, in that it comes out of occupational safety regimes and out of the Directive era, it admits cost, effort, and time into the judgement of how far to go, and it produces a defensible stopping point on economic grounds." (13)
findings.fix: Reinstate his connectives. "Recognition is not incorporation, which means the entry supports a submission and it does not create a regulation" (11) becomes "Recognition is not incorporation. This means that the entry supports a submission, however it does not create a regulation." Open several of the contrast paragraphs with "However," and several of the additive ones with "Furthermore," or "Additionally," and close at least one section with "Ultimately,".

findings.problem: Slide headlines are aphoristic and literary, where the corpus uses flat descriptive noun phrases. Draft: "Nobody Fails an Audit for Not Owning the Standard" (2), "Ninety Minutes, Thirty-Five of Them Yours" (4), "The File Is the Argument" (5), "A File, Not a Folder" (6), "Ten Clauses, and the Three People Skip" (7), "The Plan Decides the Answer Before You Know It" (9), "The Order of Priority Is an Order, Not a Menu" (22), "7.5 and 7.6, the Two Clauses Procedures Stop Short Of" (24), "The MDR Plumbing That Clause 10 Has to Connect To" (33), "The Interfaces That Get Audited" (34). The corpus headers are "Data Quality", "Data Bias", "Data Security", "Data Provenance", "Labeling and Transparency", "Managing Algorithm Changes (Predetermined Change Control Plans)", "The Foundational Role of Data", "Navigating Privacy Regulations (HIPAA & GDPR)" - no wordplay, no X-not-Y. The draft is inconsistent with itself, because slide 11 gets it right with "The Legal Position", "The Practical Position" and "Recognition and Incorporation".
findings.fix: Flatten them to the slide-11 pattern: "The Risk Management File and Traceability" (6), "The Risk Management Plan and Its Seven Required Elements" (9), "The Order of Priority for Risk Control" (22), "Clauses 7.5 and 7.6" (24), "Clause 10 and the MDR Post-Market Obligations" (33), "Common Risk Management Findings" (2), "Session Agenda and Timing" (4).

findings.problem: "is worth [verb]ing" is an 11-instance authorial tic with zero occurrences in the corpus: "it is worth naming before we go anywhere else" (2), "There are 2 structural points here that are worth saying out loud" (7), "The plumbing underneath is worth knowing" (8), "One asymmetry is worth a footnote" (13), "point 4 is worth quoting" (22), "that distinction is worth sitting with" (22), "they are worth reading out" (24), "The pattern is worth saying plainly" (30), "What V4 added is worth saying out loud" (30), "they are worth reading in order" (36), "The fourth one is the subtle one and it is worth 20 seconds" (20). "plainly" (3 uses) and "out loud" (2 uses) are likewise absent from the corpus.
findings.fix: Replace with his own flagging phrases, which the draft already uses at the right density: "It is important to note that", "It should be noted that", "I want to highlight", "I would like to take a moment to discuss", "You will note". For example "One asymmetry is worth a footnote." becomes "It should be noted that there is one asymmetry here." And "point 4 is worth quoting" becomes "I want to highlight the specific wording of point 4, because it leaves very little room."

findings.problem: The "if you take one thing away" device is used four times, which reads as a tic, and it is not a device the corpus uses at all: "If you carry a single idea out of the next 13 minutes, carry this one" (21), "If you take one slide home from today, take this one." (23), "If you only do 1 of these, do the second one" (37), "If you take one idea out of today, take this one." (39). Related self-referential asides also have no corpus precedent: "it is the slide people tend to photograph" (30), "this is the page people keep" (37), "This is the single highest-yield slide in this first section" (9).
findings.fix: Keep one, at slide 39, and rewrite the other three in his voice. Slide 23 becomes "I want to highlight Clause 7.2, because it is the requirement I see missed most often." Slide 21 becomes "It is critical that manufacturers recognize that 7.3, 7.4 and Clause 8 are three different questions." Slide 37 becomes "It is important to note that of these ten items, the verification of effectiveness records are the ones I would address first."

findings.problem: "I want to kill a zombie while we are here. The 7 content deviations that manufacturers still cite belong to EN ISO 14971:2012..." This colloquial flourish is well outside the corpus register. His closest equivalents are plain and hedged: "I want to take a moment to discuss some of the common myths and misconceptions", "This is a very basic misconception, and most senior regulatory team members will recognize this as a common misconception among younger regulatory teams".
findings.fix: "I would like to take a moment to address a common misconception before we move on. It is important to note that the 7 content deviations that manufacturers still cite belong to EN ISO 14971:2012, which was withdrawn, with conflicting national standards withdrawn by 30 June 2020."

findings.problem: "This last exercise is individual work, and that is deliberate, because a plan that belongs to the room belongs to nobody." A chiasmus. Nothing of this literary register appears anywhere in the corpus; the nearest thing he writes is workmanlike ("Just because you receive clearance does not mean that there is nothing left to do, it is actually just the opposite").
findings.fix: "This last exercise is individual work, and that is deliberate. It is important to note that an action item without a single owner is very rarely completed, which is why I am asking each of you to write your own."

findings.problem: A bare semicolon used for rhetorical antithesis: "Risk files do not fail because a procedure is missing; they fail on traceability and on arithmetic that cannot be defended." Every one of the corpus's 7 semicolons introduces "however" or a similar connector ("This program is entirely voluntary; however, it can provide manufacturers with clear regulatory guidance"). The draft has exactly one semicolon in 12,900 words and it is the one construction he does not use.
findings.fix: "It is important to note that risk files do not typically fail because a procedure is missing. They fail on traceability, and on arithmetic that cannot be defended."

findings.problem: Metaphor and epigram in place of plain statement. "if you cannot say which half of the number is engineering and which half is clinical, you have one number wearing two hats" (20); "An estimate with no stated basis is not a weak estimate, it is the finding." (3); "'Pump fails' is a state, it is not a sequence" (20); "Clause 4.5 is where the obligation actually bites" (6); "What the file may not be is unwalkable" (6). The corpus reaches for flat exposition instead, for example "The impact of poor data quality is profound. It directly undermines the reliability and trustworthiness of the AI medical device."
findings.fix: "one number wearing two hats" becomes "a single number that cannot be defended on either basis." "An estimate with no stated basis is not a weak estimate, it is the finding." becomes "It is important to note that an estimate with no stated basis will itself be written up as a finding." "where the obligation actually bites" becomes "where the actual obligation is stipulated."

findings.problem: The opening block is correct but has three editorializing paragraphs bolted into it before "So with that said, lets dive in.", beginning "I want to say the promise of today plainly. We are not here to learn the standard, we are here to work a file..." The corpus opening is a single dense paragraph of scope ("We will discuss... We will also identify... Finally, we will discuss...") running straight into "So with that said, lets dive in", with no interpolated commentary and certainly no "we are not here to X, we are here to Y".
findings.fix: Fold the material into the existing scope paragraph and drop the antithesis: "We will also work through the materials provided, which include the participant handout as your reference, the hands-on exercise pack, and the Excel toolkit that you will take back to your desk. It should be noted that this session assumes you already have a risk file in place. If you are starting from nothing, the risk management plan comes first, and the 'RM Plan' sheet in the toolkit is where to start. So with that said, lets dive in."

findings.problem: The closing formula is correctly placed and used once, but the antithesis tic has been inserted into it, deforming the borrowed frame: "So with that said, it is easy to recognize why the file itself, and not the activity behind it, is what has to carry the argument for manufacturers who intend to defend their risk management before a notified body or an FDA investigator." The corpus frame is smooth: "So with that said, it is easy to recognize why it is so critical to understand these distinctions for manufacturers who intend to navigate the 510(k) process successfully."
findings.fix: "So with that said, it is easy to recognize why it is so critical to maintain a traceable and defensible risk management file for manufacturers who intend to defend their risk management before a notified body or an FDA investigator."

findings.problem: "if you search the 78 pages of Compliance Program 7382.850 for the string 14971 you get 0 hits." A digit for zero in running prose. The corpus uses digits for counted quantities ("only 7 FDA cleared disposable endoscopes", "2 warning letters", "14 presubmission packages") but never a bare 0 of this kind.
findings.fix: "...you will find that the standard is not mentioned a single time." Or "you get zero hits."

summary:
Needs work. The scaffolding is right and the stock phrases are, notably, NOT over-used - but the prose between them belongs to a different, more literary writer.

What passes: the opening formula is reproduced faithfully on slide 1 and appears nowhere else; the closing pair ("So with that said, it is easy to recognize why..." / "This concludes the presentation portion of this discussion. I want to thank each of you who attended, and I welcome any questions you may have at this time.") sits correctly and only on slide 39; "lets dive in" keeps his missing apostrophe. On the over-imitation question specifically, the density is fine and if anything slightly under the corpus: "important to note" appears 6 times in 12,895 words against 6 times in 11,242 corpus words, "important to know" 3 vs 1, "should be noted" 0 vs 3 - so the total flagging-phrase load is about 9 per 12,900 words against roughly 11 per 11,200. No parody risk there; if anything he should be flagging more often, because the draft has substituted "is worth saying/naming/knowing" (11 instances, zero in corpus) for those markers. "we can move on to" (5), "may be asking" (3), "I would like to take a moment" (2) and "I want to highlight" (2) are all within range. Slide 11's header block and slide 14's audience-question pivot are genuinely well matched.

What fails, in order of weight. First, antithesis saturation: "rather than" runs at 2.0 per 1,000 words against his 0.2, and the bare "X, not Y" turn appears roughly 14 more times. It is in the slide titles, in the body, and it has even been wedged into the closing formula. Second, verbless fragments for emphasis ("Shall, and in this order.", "Not cost, not schedule, not manufacturability.", "Read it.") - the corpus has none; its short sentences are all complete instructional imperatives. Third, inverted pronoun discipline: "manufacturers" collapses from 6.2 to 1.2 per 1,000 words while "you" more than doubles to 12.8, so regulatory obligations he assigns to manufacturers are delivered as second-person coaching ("The sources you are required to collect from...", "7.5 requires you to review..."). Fourth, British spelling throughout - colour, categorisation, minimisation, generalisation, labelling, analysed, plasticiser, behaviour, judgement, centre, recognised - where he writes American without exception ("labeling" 17 times, "behavior", "minimize", "recognize", "generalizability").
