Fifth, his lists have been dissolved into inline colon-prose; slide 6 runs a set of capitalised questions after a colon with the question marks removed, a construction that exists nowhere in the corpus, where every "include:" is followed by real bullets. Sixth, the connective tissue is someone else's: zero "Furthermore", "Additionally", "In addition", "Ultimately" or "This means" (6/5/2/6/2 in corpus), only 3 "However," against 11, and 11 uses of "which means" (zero in corpus).

On top of that are the local flourishes no line of the corpus would support: "I want to kill a zombie while we are here" (12), "a plan that belongs to the room belongs to nobody" (36), "you have one number wearing two hats" (20), "Clause 4.5 is where the obligation actually bites" (6), "A risk file is an argument, not an archive" (39), plus a bare rhetorical semicolon on slide 2 and the "if you take one thing away" device used four separate times. Fixing the six pervasive items would move this most of the way; the rest are line edits.

COVERAGE is clean: all 39 slides are present exactly once, each headed "SLIDE n", in order, with no duplicates and no invented slides. FIDELITY to the speaker notes is high overall — the heavy citation slides (11, 12, 13, 14, 29, 30, 33, 34, 38) reproduce every clause number, recognition number, Federal Register cite, OJ reference, decision number, article, annex point and date correctly, and in two places the draft is actually MORE accurate than the notes (slide 12 correctly lists points 1, 2, 6 and 7 as not covered by Annex ZA, where the notes omit point 6; slide 29 correctly includes GSPR 22.1, which the notes drop). No clause number, CFR citation, regulation article or standard designation was found altered, transposed or mis-stated anywhere in the deck.

The problems are: (1) two invented speaker identities on slide 1 ("Laura", "Jordan Elder") that appear nowhere in the source and that the speaker would read aloud verbatim; (2) an invented and incorrect column count on slide 18; (3) the whole "trap to watch for" paragraph of slide 27's notes is dropped, so three structural findings are never flagged to the room; (4) slide 26 rewrites the excerpt's location in a way that contradicts slide 27's "you have the excerpt and nothing else"; (5) slide 30 inverts Team-NB section 5.5, presenting the guidance's requirements ("no green zone", "no RPN alone") as the pitfalls themselves; (6) slide 19 generalises a severity comparison across all three model rows in a way the slide table contradicts; and (7) about six smaller drops of concrete detail from the notes (the A/B/C exercise mapping, "section 6" as the compression target, "two or three hands", "nine inputs", "Section 9 is the Annex XVI provision", "(Section 3)", "the stated risk control is not identified").

findings.problem: The transcript invents two names that appear nowhere in the on-screen text or the speaker notes: "Hello and thank you Laura for that introduction" and "My name is Jordan Elder". The source slide names only the organisation — "Elder Consulting, LLC" — and never a presenter or an introducer. Because the speaker reads this verbatim, they would say a name that may not be theirs and thank a person who may not exist.
findings.fix: Replace with placeholders the presenter fills in, e.g. "Thank you for that introduction, and thank you to those joining us for today's presentation. I am [PRESENTER NAME] of Elder Consulting, and today we are going to discuss ISO 14971 in practice..." — or drop the introducer thanks entirely, since the notes only say "Welcome."

findings.problem: Invented figure: "There are 13 columns there, running from the device function or part all the way through to the status." The notes say nothing about a column count, and the on-screen table does not support the number: from "Device function or part" through "Status" there are 12 fields (13 only if the "ID" row is included, which the sentence explicitly excludes).
findings.fix: Cut the count. The notes for this slide are only "Put it up and say nothing for ten seconds. Let them read it." Use: "This is HZ-15, exactly as it appears in the file, and it is HZ-15 in the Excel toolkit as well, so you will be able to find it in situ afterwards. Read it."

findings.problem: The entire final paragraph of the speaker notes is dropped and therefore never said: "The trap to watch for: groups that only critique the numbers. The deeper findings are structural: the order of priority not worked, the effectiveness verification absent, the disclosure obligation unmet." The transcript ends at the 9-minute/5-minute timing and the stall hint, with no mention of the numbers-only trap or the three structural findings it points at.
findings.fix: Add before the timing paragraph: "One trap to watch for as you work: groups tend to critique only the numbers. The deeper findings in this excerpt are structural — the order of priority was not worked, the verification of effectiveness is absent, and the disclosure obligation is unmet."

findings.problem: The transcript says the exercise pack contains the answers: "what you are working from is exercise pack page 4, which is a real-looking risk file excerpt together with the deficiencies a notified body would raise against it." The on-screen subtitle describes the SEGMENT ("A real-looking risk file excerpt, and the deficiencies a notified body would raise"), not the contents of page 4. This contradicts slide 27, which tells the room "you have the excerpt in front of you and nothing else", and it would have participants looking for a findings list that is not there.
findings.fix: "...what you are working from is exercise pack page 4, which is a real-looking risk file excerpt. By the end of the fourteen minutes we will have the deficiencies a notified body would raise against it — but they come from you, not from the page."

findings.problem: The transcript inverts what Team-NB section 5.5 says: "section 5.5 is a named list of the common pitfalls in risk management that notified bodies observe. It expects you to state whether your risk management process is based on EN ISO 14971, and the pitfalls include: no acceptance on the Risk Priority Number, or RPN, alone, no green zone, each risk decided individually against predefined criteria, a statement that the clinical benefits outweigh all of the residual risks, and 3 distinct risk assessments..." The notes present these as the guidance's EXPECTATIONS, not as pitfalls. As written, "no green zone" and "each risk decided individually" are stated to be pitfalls, which reverses their meaning.
findings.fix: "...section 5.5 is a named list of the common pitfalls in risk management that notified bodies observe. The guidance expects you to state whether your risk management process is based on EN ISO 14971; it expects no acceptance on RPN alone and no green zone, each risk decided individually against predefined criteria, a statement that the clinical benefits outweigh all of the residual risks, and three distinct risk assessments covering design, production and process, and clinical or application — which catches the firms that have only ever done the design one."

findings.problem: The transcript over-generalises a comparison the slide table contradicts: "The hazard category is the same in all three, and yet under-infusion carries a lower severity and a different P2." Row 2 on the slide is an under-infusion row with severity 4 — the same severity as the row 1 bolus it is being contrasted with. Only row 3 has a lower severity (3). The notes scope this correctly to "comparing rows 2 and 3".
findings.fix: Scope it to the rows that actually differ: "Hold the second and third rows against each other. The hazard category is the same, but the third row's under-infusion carries a lower severity and a different P2, because loss of therapy is usually detectable and recoverable, whereas the bolus is neither."

findings.problem: The notes' explicit exercise mapping is dropped. Notes: "Each one maps to an exercise: A is the chain, B is the red-team, C is the plan." The transcript flattens this to "each one of them maps onto an exercise or a section", so the room never hears which objective belongs to which exercise.
findings.fix: "...and each one maps onto an exercise: A is the chain, B is the red-team, and C is the plan."

findings.problem: The notes name the specific section to be sacrificed: "If we overrun, the compression comes out of section 6, not out of the exercises." The transcript generalises to "the compression comes out of the presented material and not out of the exercises", dropping the identification of section 6.
findings.fix: "If we overrun, the compression comes out of section 6, the closing-the-loop section, and not out of the exercises."

findings.problem: The notes give the expected response to the d) poll — "Usually two or three hands" — and the transcript replaces it with a content-free line: "That is about what I see in most rooms, and it is a gap that a great deal of the industry is carrying." The concrete figure, which is the point of asking, is never said.
findings.fix: "That is about what I see in most rooms — usually two or three hands out of a room this size, and that gap is one a great deal of the industry is carrying."

findings.problem: The notes' count is dropped: "The toolkit's Residual Risk sheet lists the nine inputs a credible Clause 8 evaluation considers" becomes "lists the inputs that a credible Clause 8 evaluation considers". (Flagging both ways: the notes say nine, but the on-screen table lists only eight items, so the source itself is inconsistent — the count needs settling before it is spoken or omitted.)
findings.fix: Reconcile the source first, then state it, e.g. "The toolkit's Residual Risk sheet lists the eight inputs a credible Clause 8 evaluation considers" — matching however many the slide table ends up carrying.

findings.problem: Two details from the notes on the Annex XIV numbering trap are dropped. The notes explain WHY the cross-reference is wrong: "Section 9 is the Annex XVI provision; the benefit-risk sections are 1 and 8." The transcript keeps only "where the benefit-risk sections are 1 and 8", so the audience is told the citation is wrong but not what Section 9 actually is.
findings.fix: "...still refers to the benefit-risk ratio in Sections 1 and 9 of Annex I. Section 9 is the Annex XVI provision on devices without an intended medical purpose; the benefit-risk sections are 1 and 8. That cross-reference was never corrected, unlike the identical error in Article 88(1), which was."

findings.problem: The Annex II point 5 row is truncated. The slide reads: "The technical documentation contains the benefit-risk analysis (Sections 1 and 8) and the solutions adopted and the results of the risk management (Section 3)." The transcript drops the "(Section 3)" attachment, saying only "...together with the solutions adopted and the results of the risk management".
findings.fix: "...has to contain the benefit-risk analysis in Sections 1 and 8 of Annex I, together with the solutions adopted and the results of the risk management under Section 3."

findings.problem: The model deficiency wording drops a clause of the source finding. The slide reads "The stated risk control is not identified and is not traceable to a verification of implementation or of effectiveness (7.2)"; the transcript says only "The stated control of 'mitigated by design' is not traceable to a verification of implementation or of effectiveness, which is 7.2", losing the "is not identified" defect (i.e. that "mitigated by design" does not name a control at all).
findings.fix: "The stated control, 'mitigated by design', does not identify a risk control measure at all, and is not traceable to a verification of implementation or of effectiveness, which is 7.2."

findings.problem: The transcript closes with an added sentence that is not in the notes and that muddles the deck's own argument: "So with that said, it is easy to recognize why the file itself, and not the activity behind it, is what has to carry the argument..." Slide 11 makes the opposite emphasis — "the standard is not [mandatory], the activity is" — and the deck's one idea is that the file records the argument, not that the file matters more than the activity.
findings.fix: Cut the sentence. End on the notes' own structure: "That concludes the presentation portion. I want to thank each of you who attended, and I welcome any questions you may have at this time."

findings.problem: Slide 16 gives away Exercise A's model answer before the room has worked it. Slide 16: "A single hazard – say stored energy in a compliant fluid path – reaches several hazardous situations by several sequences, and each carries its own probability, which is why collapsing several sequences into one row makes a probability estimate impossible to defend." Slide 19's model answer is that exact hazard: "The hazard is stored mechanical energy in the compliant fluid path... One line about the pumping mechanism becomes 3 rows, because there are 3 distinct hazardous situations reached by 3 distinct sequences." And slide 20's first pattern is "rebuilding one row instead of several." Two slides later the speaker claims the opposite: slide 18, "I am not going to pre-empt any of the findings, because the whole value of the next 10 minutes is in you finding them yourselves." The chunk-4 writer used the answer as the teaching illustration and then promised not to pre-empt it.
findings.fix: Change slide 16's illustrative hazard to something outside HZ-15 and outside the pump's fluid path (e.g. "a sharp edge on a reusable handpiece reaches a cut during handling by one sequence and a contaminated-wound infection by another"), and drop the count "several hazardous situations by several sequences" so the structural answer is not handed over. Keep slide 18's promise intact.

findings.problem: The single most important instruction in the takeaways points at the wrong list item. Slide 37: "If you only do 1 of these, do the second one, the verification of effectiveness records." Item 2 of the list is "Add a 7.6 completeness step to the procedure, and run it over the acceptable rows as well as the ones you argued about." Verification of effectiveness is item 3. A listener following along on the printed page hears "the second one" and marks the wrong action on the page the speaker has just called "the page people keep."
findings.fix: Say "do number three, the verification of effectiveness records" — or, better, drop the ordinal entirely and name it only: "If you only do one of these, do the verification of effectiveness records." Ordinals into a read-aloud numbered list are fragile; the name is not.

findings.problem: The toolkit claim does not match the six checks it refers to. Slide 36: "The Dashboard sheet in the Excel toolkit computes 5 of those 6 for you once you have loaded your own rows, and the sixth, the Clause 8 evaluation, is the one it leaves blank on purpose." None of the six prompts just read out is a Clause 8 evaluation — they are 4.4 d), 7.2 effectiveness, the cost justification under Annex I point 2, the 7.6 completeness step, the 10.3/10.4 complaint trace, and the risk-plan-versus-clinical-evaluation-plan agreement. The sixth is the last of those, not Clause 8.
findings.fix: Either make the sixth prompt the Clause 8 one ("Does your Clause 8 overall residual risk evaluation exist as an evaluation rather than a roll-up?"), or fix the sentence to match what was read: "The Dashboard computes five of those six; the sixth, whether your risk plan criteria and your clinical evaluation plan parameters agree, is a document comparison no spreadsheet can make for you."

findings.problem: Three numbers in one sentence contradict each other. Slide 36: "which is 16 rows with 2 of them deliberately defective, one control missing its verification of effectiveness, one justification citing cost, and one open post-production item. The facilitator guide names all 5 of those." Two defective rows are announced, three defects are then listed, and the total is given as five. Spoken, the audience hears the count change twice in fifteen seconds.
findings.fix: Pick one count and carry it: "sixteen rows, three of them deliberately defective — one control missing its verification of effectiveness, one justification citing cost, and one open post-production item. The facilitator guide names all three."

findings.problem: The Exercise C duration changes across the 35/36 chunk boundary. Slide 35: "We have 8 minutes for it." Slide 36, the very next thing said: "The framing that makes the next 5 minutes useful..." and "You have 5 minutes." Slide 4's agenda supports 5: "the last 8 minutes are Exercise C, your own 30-day plan, the takeaways, and any questions" — eight minutes covers the exercise plus the close, not the writing.
findings.fix: On slide 35 say "We have about eight minutes for this and the close, and five of them are yours to write in," so the 5 on slide 36 lands as a restatement rather than a correction.

findings.problem: Three different and non-overlapping sets of "four things" are each framed as the canonical four, so the listener never knows which four to hold. Slide 2: "The gap then opens in four fairly predictable places. Traceability breaks at the control, estimates have no stated basis, the Clause 10 log is either empty or entirely historical, and the acceptability criteria turn out to have been reverse-engineered." Slide 5: "the aim is to fix the 4 places where risk files reliably break, which include: the plan written too late, the chain collapsed into a single row, the estimate with no stated basis, and the file that is a folder rather than an argument." Slide 20 then offers a third four ("These are the recurring patterns"), which slide 21 canonises as "the 4 things the room reliably gets wrong." Only "no stated basis" appears in more than one.
findings.fix: Fix one list of four as the deck's spine — slide 5's is the best fit for the arc — and re-label the others so they cannot be mistaken for it: slide 2 becomes "the four places findings come from," slide 20 becomes "the four mistakes this exercise produces every time." Cross-reference them explicitly ("these are the exercise-level versions of the four we opened with") rather than letting three unrelated fours float.

findings.problem: The reviewer traversal is delivered as a fresh revelation for the third time, once per chunk that touches it. Slide 2: "A reviewer pulls one hazard and walks it end to end, asks where a probability number came from, asks for the effectiveness record rather than the implementation record, and asks what post-market data changed after the file was signed." Slide 6: "The questions a reviewer arrives with are predictable, and the places the file has to answer them from include: Where did this hazard come from... Where did this number come from... What did you do about it, and does it work... And finally, what has changed since." Slide 30: "What a reviewer does with a risk file is not a document review, it is a traversal, it is 6 moves in a fixed order... Then they ask for the effectiveness record rather than the implementation record." Slide 30 even repeats slide 2's clause verbatim while presenting the whole thing as "the generalisation out of Exercise B."
findings.fix: Make slide 2 the only full statement, keep slide 6 as a pure file-location mapping (drop the reviewer framing, lead with "the file has to answer from"), and open slide 30 as an explicit callback that earns its detail from the exercise: "You have now been the reviewer for fourteen minutes, so the four moves I sketched at the start can be named properly, and there are six of them." Delete the repeated "effectiveness record rather than the implementation record" clause from one of the two.

findings.problem: The Team-NB citation, its date, and its pitfall list are delivered near-verbatim twice, sixteen slides apart, with the RPN acronym expanded both times. Slide 14: "Team-NB's best practice guidance on technical documentation, now at V4 adopted 21 April 2026, says plainly that the MDR does not permit risk acceptance on Risk Priority Number, or RPN, alone or on a 'green' zone, and that acceptability must be decided individually against predefined criteria." Slide 30: "Team-NB's best practice guidance on technical documentation, now at V4, adopted 21 April 2026... the pitfalls include: no acceptance on the Risk Priority Number, or RPN, alone, no green zone, each risk decided individually against predefined criteria."
findings.fix: Keep the full introduction and the date at slide 30, where the pitfall list does real work. At slide 14 compress to the substance without the citation apparatus: "and the notified bodies' own position paper says the MDR does not permit acceptance on an RPN alone or on a green zone — I will come back to that document at the end of Exercise B." Expand RPN once, at slide 14.

findings.problem: Two adjacent structural points from slide 7 are re-delivered on slide 24 as new material, one of them word for word. Slide 7: "Clause 7 runs to 7.6, not to 7.5, so if your procedure stops at risks arising from risk control measures you are missing completeness of risk control altogether. Clause 6 routes an acceptable risk straight to 7.6 and tells you to treat the estimated risk as the residual risk, which means 7.6 applies to every hazardous situation you identified, acceptable or not. Manufacturers assume the acceptable ones drop out of the process, and they do not." Slide 24: "an acceptable risk goes straight to 7.6, and its estimated risk is treated as the residual risk. So 7.6 applies to every hazardous situation in your file... because Clause 7 runs to 7.6, not to 7.5." Slide 24 at least signals the callback ("Remember the routing out of Clause 6 here") and then ignores its own signal by explaining it from scratch. Slide 21 makes it a third time: "Clause 7 on its own runs to 6 parts, which is more parts than most of the procedures I read actually account for."
findings.fix: Cut the explanation from slide 7 down to a flag only ("and note that Clause 7 has a sixth part that most procedures stop short of — we will work it in the risk control section"), and let slide 24 carry the full mechanism once, since that is where the fix lands. Remove the duplicated part-count remark from slide 21.

findings.problem: Seven slides each claim to be the one thing to take away, which cancels all of them and undercuts the real close. Slide 9: "This is the single highest-yield slide in this first section." Slide 21: "If you carry a single idea out of the next 13 minutes, carry this one." Slide 23: "If you take one slide home from today, take this one." Slide 25: "This slide is the conceptual centre of the section." Slide 30: "it is the slide people tend to photograph." Slide 37: "this is the page people keep." Slide 39: "If you take one idea out of today, take this one." Slides 23 and 39 make outright competing claims to being the single takeaway of the whole session.
findings.fix: Reserve the absolute form for slide 39 alone. Downgrade the others to section-scoped or delete: slide 23 becomes "This is the slide that decides whether the section holds together," slide 21 keeps "carry one idea out of the next thirteen minutes" only if slide 25 drops "conceptual centre," and slides 9, 30 and 37 lose the framing entirely and rely on their content.

findings.problem: The final sentence of the deck is unspeakable and contradicts the central claim of slide 11. Slide 39: "So with that said, it is easy to recognize why the file itself, and not the activity behind it, is what has to carry the argument for manufacturers who intend to defend their risk management before a notified body or an FDA investigator." It is a 41-word sentence built on the limp "it is easy to recognize why," and its file-not-activity contrast inverts slide 11's whole FDA argument: "the standard is not [mandatory], and the activity is" and "An observation is written against the clause, not against ISO 14971." Slide 39 also already had the right closing line three paragraphs earlier: "A risk file is an argument, not an archive."
findings.fix: Delete the sentence. End on the promise the opening made: "We said at the start that we were not here to learn the standard, we were here to work a file. You have taken a row apart, rebuilt it, written the deficiency, and written your own thirty days. A risk file is an argument, not an archive. Thank you — I welcome your questions."

findings.problem: The close is buried. Slide 39 opens with the deck's best line — "If you take one idea out of today, take this one. A risk file is an argument, not an archive" — and then runs roughly 350 further words: three pre-answered FAQs, an offer to walk a delegate's row, a legal disclaimer, and the garbled summary sentence. The last thing the room actually hears before questions is a disclaimer and a subordinate clause, not the argument the opening promised.
findings.fix: Move the three pre-answered questions to the front of the Q&A, after the close, and flag them as such ("before I take yours, here are the three that come every time"). Keep the disclaimer as one short line earlier in the slide. End the spoken deck on "an argument, not an archive."

findings.problem: Slides 33 and 34 are a citation blizzard that cannot be followed by ear. Slide 33 alone speaks Article 10(2), Article 10(9)(e), Annex I point 3 sub-points (e) and (f), Article 83(3)(a), Annex II point 5, Annex III point 1(b), Article 86(1)(a), Article 88(1), Article 61(10), Annex XIV Part B point 8, Recital 33, Corrigendum C2, "Annex III from 1.1 and 1.2 to 1 and 2", and Annex XIV Part B point 6.1(d). Slide 34 adds "Annex VII 4.5.4(c) and 4.5.5, Annex XIV Part A 1(a) and recital 33" and "MDR Annex I 17.1, 17.2, 17.4 and 18.8, and MDCG 2019-16 revision 1." The worst single sentence is slide 33's numbering trap, whose entire point depends on the listener holding two invisible numbers apart: "Annex XIV Part B point 6.1(d) still refers to the benefit-risk ratio in Sections 1 and 9 of Annex I, where the benefit-risk sections are 1 and 8, and that cross-reference was never corrected, unlike the identical error in Article 88(1) which was."
findings.fix: Speak the obligation and leave the citation on the slide. For each provision use the pattern "the law requires X — the article is on the slide and in the handout." Cut slide 33 to the four joints that matter (Article 10(2), Annex I point 3, Article 83(3), Annex III point 1(b)) and move the rest to the handout. Replace the numbering-trap sentence with "two cross-references in the MDR point at the wrong Annex I sections. If your SOP quotes Annex III section 1.1, or Annex XIV's benefit-risk cross-reference, check both against the handout before your next audit — the details are on the slide."

findings.problem: A single sentence on slide 14 runs to roughly 95 words and cannot be said in one breath: "Whether benefit-risk is expected for an individual risk is the one that changes your record count, because Annex I point 4 speaks of the residual risk associated with each hazard, and Team-NB's best practice guidance on technical documentation, now at V4 adopted 21 April 2026, says plainly that the MDR does not permit risk acceptance on Risk Priority Number, or RPN, alone or on a 'green' zone, and that acceptability must be decided individually against predefined criteria, wording that is identical in V3 and V4 and has therefore been their position for over a year." The sentence before it is another 65-word chain ("On post-market information, the EU routes it through Article 83(3)(a)...").
findings.fix: Break into three: "Whether benefit-risk is expected for an individual risk changes your record count. Annex I point 4 speaks of the residual risk associated with each hazard — each one, individually. The notified bodies' own guidance says the same: no acceptance on an RPN alone, no green zone, every risk judged against predefined criteria." Same treatment for the post-market sentence: one clause per regulator, one sentence each.

findings.problem: Slide 25's closing sentence is a roughly 90-word, eight-item list delivered as one breath: "The toolkit's Residual Risk sheet lists the inputs that a credible Clause 8 evaluation considers, and those include: risks that share a single common cause, conflicting requirements between risk controls, the number and nature of the warnings that safety rests on, comparison with similar devices and the state of the art, the clinical benefit and the benefit-risk conclusion, information from production and post-production, disclosure of significant residual risks in the accompanying information, and the conclusion itself, recorded against the criteria the plan declared and signed by someone who holds the authority to sign it." Eight parallel items with no landing points is unlistenable and unmemorable. Slide 11 ("those clauses include: 4.1.2 b), 7.1, the design, purchasing, production and monitoring equipment clauses at 7.3 through 7.6, and 8.2") and slide 7 (the 80-word "usual state" chain) have the same problem.
findings.fix: Speak three items and point at the sheet for the rest: "A credible Clause 8 evaluation considers three things above all — risks that share a single common cause, conflicting requirements between controls, and how many warnings the safety case is resting on. The Residual Risk sheet lists the full set of inputs." Break slide 7's "usual state" chain into three short sentences and let slide 11's clause numbers stay on screen.

findings.problem: Slide 13 opens with a backward reference to something never said. "The cleanest way to make this distinction land is by what is absent from the regulation." No distinction has been introduced — slide 12 ended on Annex ZA scope and MDCG 2021-5, and ALARP versus AFAP appears nowhere before this sentence. A listener spends the first twenty seconds of the slide hunting for an antecedent. The slide title "ALARP and AFAP" supplies it visually, which is exactly the punctuation-the-listener-cannot-hear failure.
findings.fix: Name the distinction in the first clause: "There is one distinction in this section that changes how far you have to go, and it is the difference between ALARP and AFAP. The cleanest way to make it land is by what is absent from the regulation."

findings.problem: MDR is expanded four times, once per chunk that needs it, as if the audience were meeting it fresh each time. Slide 1: "the European Union Medical Device Regulation, or MDR." Slide 12: "is a harmonised standard for the Medical Device Regulation, or MDR." Slide 27: "the point in Annex I of the EU Medical Device Regulation, or MDR." Slide 33: "obligations under the Medical Device Regulation, or MDR." GSPR is expanded three times (slides 4, 12, 36), RPN twice (14, 30), PSUR twice (3, 33), AFAP twice (13, and slide 32's "Your AFAP position, meaning risk reduced as far as possible"). Each re-expansion tells the room the speaker has forgotten what he already said.
findings.fix: Expand each acronym exactly once, at first use, and use the short form thereafter: MDR at slide 1, GSPR at slide 4, PSUR at slide 3, RPN at slide 14, AFAP at slide 13. Delete the later expansions at slides 12, 27, 32, 33 and 36.

findings.problem: "MDR" is used in its second, unrelated sense six slides after the deck warned about it, with no reminder. Slide 20: "An 'MDR reportable event' is not a harm, while 'hypotension requiring intervention' is." The only flag came on slide 14: "Medical Device Reporting under 21 CFR 803, which is a second and entirely different MDR." Everywhere else in the deck MDR means the Medical Device Regulation, and slide 20 sits in the middle of a run of Annex I citations. Spoken, with the quotation marks inaudible, the room hears the European regulation. The quote marks around "Reportable incident", "complaint" and "recall" in the preceding sentence are silent for the same reason.
findings.fix: Say the words out: "A reportable event under Medical Device Reporting is not a harm; hypotension requiring intervention is." And voice the quoted terms as quoted: "The words reportable incident, complaint and recall all name consequences of harm. None of them is a harm."

findings.problem: A promise made in the opening is never kept. Slide 2, after the show of hands: "I will come back to what this room has told me as we work." Nothing later refers to the poll. Slide 9's second show of hands is closed with a generic "That is about what I see in most rooms" and does not connect to it. Slide 21's "the 4 things the room reliably gets wrong" refers to slide 20's patterns, not the poll. Slide 37 comes closest and pointedly cites the wrong source: "It is the finding that appears most often in the files I review" — the files he reviews, not the hands this room raised.
findings.fix: Pay it off at slide 37, where the verification-of-effectiveness recommendation lands: "Remember the hands that stayed up at the start of this session, when I asked whose finding was verification of effectiveness. That is why this is the one to do first." One sentence closes the loop and makes the opening poll load-bearing.

findings.problem: Register and citation numbers are written to be read, not spoken. Slide 11: "It entered the database on 23 December 2019 and was published in Recognition List Number 053 at 85 FR 17584 on 30 March 2020, replacing recognition 5-40 for the 2007 edition, and it was still unchanged in Recognition List Number 066 of 24 August 2026." Said aloud that is "eighty-five F R one seven five eight four" plus five other numbers in one sentence. Slide 12 does the same with "Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2022/757 of 11 May 2022, published in the Official Journal L 138 on 17 May 2022... Decision 2022/729... generated on 17 June 2026."
findings.fix: Speak one number per fact and leave the rest on the slide: "ISO 14971:2019 is recognised in full — recognition five dash one two five — and that has been stable since 2019. The Federal Register citation and the list numbers are on the slide." Same for slide 12: "harmonised since May 2022, by the implementing decision cited on the slide."

findings.problem: The exercise clock is declared started and then the speaker keeps talking. Slide 18: "That is your 10 minutes, starting now. I am not going to pre-empt any of the findings..." — followed by a further paragraph ("I will be circulating while you work, and the two things I will be pushing on are...") before the "[TABLE WORK - 10 MINUTES. CIRCULATE.]" cue. Slide 28 gets the same moment right: "Your 9 minutes starts now." immediately followed by its table-work cue.
findings.fix: Move "That is your ten minutes, starting now" to the end, immediately before the cue, with the circulating remarks ahead of it — matching slide 28.

findings.problem: A show-of-hands cue follows a question the room cannot answer with hands. Slide 9: "So let me ask the room. Does your plan actually say what you do when you cannot estimate a probability?" then "[PAUSE FOR SHOW OF HANDS]". Slide 2 gets the construction right — "Hands up if you have ever had a risk-management finding. Keep them up if the finding was verification of effectiveness" — so the room has been trained on one pattern and is then given a yes/no question with no instruction.
findings.fix: Phrase it for hands: "Hands up if your plan actually says what you do when a probability cannot be estimated." Keep the cue as it is.

findings.problem: The same anecdote carries two different numbers. Slide 2: "an empty Clause 10 log on a device that has been on the market for 4 years." Slide 9: "a plan that is silent here is exactly why the Clause 10 log is still empty 3 years later." Slide 7 and slide 32 make it a third and fourth time ("Clause 10 as a whole... is very often an empty log"; "this is the clause most often found completely empty on a device that has been marketed for years"). A recurring figure that changes is heard as carelessness.
findings.fix: Fix one number and one phrasing — "four years on the market, empty log" — use it at slide 2, and reduce slides 7, 9 and 32 to bare references ("the empty Clause 10 log we opened with").

findings.problem: Bare title lines appear on some slides and not others, split exactly along chunk lines, so a presenter reading the transcript cannot tell what is spoken. Slides 2 through 14, 21 through 25 and 31 through 35 open with a standalone title line ("A File, Not a Folder", "ALARP and AFAP", "Closing the Loop"). Slides 16 through 20, 26 through 30 and 36 through 39 open straight into speech. Slide 35 has "Exercise C: Your 30-Day Plan" while the other two exercise openers, slides 15 and 26, have none.
findings.fix: Pick one convention for the whole transcript. Since the titles are on the slides already, drop the standalone title lines everywhere and let each slide open with its first spoken sentence — which is what chunks 4, 6 and 8 already do.

findings.problem: Title-case heading fragments are embedded in the spoken text, punctuated inconsistently, and could be read either as on-screen text or as script. Slide 32 has four unpunctuated heading lines: "The First Question is Whether There is a Previously Unrecognised Hazard or Hazardous Situation" with no full stop, then body text. Slide 29 uses the same device but folds it into full sentences with terminal punctuation: "The First Finding is the Major One, and it sits in the risk control row of HZ-16." One reads as a slide bullet, the other as speech.
findings.fix: Make them all speech, lower case and punctuated: "The first question is whether there is a previously unrecognised hazard or hazardous situation." The slide carries the heading; the transcript should carry only what is said.

findings.problem: The model answer loses its counting halfway through, so a listener cannot track against the "at least 6" they were promised. Slide 27 sets the target: "There are at least 6 defensible findings in the excerpt." Slide 29 numbers the first three ("The First Finding is the Major One", "The Second Finding is the Structural Twin", "The Third Finding is the One Most Rooms Miss") and then delivers four more as unlabelled paragraphs beginning "HZ-16 also records no disclosure...", "The basis for the estimate on HZ-16 is given as...", "There is no Clause 7.5 assessment...", "Finally, the general safety and performance requirement link...".
findings.fix: Number all seven aloud, or stop numbering after the third and signal the switch: "Those are the three that decide the file. There are four more, and I will take them quickly." Then "Fourth... fifth... sixth... and seventh."

findings.problem: A stated count does not match the items given. Slide 30 promises "it is 6 moves in a fixed order" and then compresses the end into "The last 2 moves are to the labelling and the clinical evaluation, and then out to the post-market data and back." That names three destinations (labelling, clinical evaluation, post-market data) for two slots, after four earlier moves. The arithmetic only works if the listener guesses which two of the three pair up.
findings.fix: Split them cleanly: "The fifth move is out to the labelling and the clinical evaluation — is the residual risk disclosed, and do the risk file criteria and the clinical evaluation parameters agree? The sixth is out to the post-market data and back."

findings.problem: The four recurring patterns are signposted for the first and fourth only, so the middle two vanish. Slide 20: "The first one I want to name is rebuilding one row instead of several..." then an unsignposted paragraph containing two patterns run together ("Writing a sequence that is only one step long... Assigning P1 and P2 without separating the evidence behind them...") and then "The fourth one is the subtle one." A listener who was counting hears one, then four.
findings.fix: Signpost all four: "The first... The second is writing a sequence that is only one step long... The third is assigning P1 and P2 without separating the evidence... The fourth is the subtle one."

findings.problem: The first pre-answered question re-delivers slide 14's first row almost verbatim, the third time the deck makes the point. Slide 14: "the EU answer is voluntary but harmonised, with a presumption of conformity for the points Annex ZA lists, while for FDA it is not incorporated into Part 820 but is a recognized consensus standard." Slide 39: "In the EU it is voluntary but harmonised, and the presumption of conformity only covers what Annex ZA lists. For FDA it is not incorporated into Part 820, it is a recognized consensus standard." Slides 11 and 12 carry the full version before either.
findings.fix: Answer it as a callback, not a re-statement: "Not as law, in either jurisdiction — that is the whole of slides eleven and twelve, and the two-column mapping is in the handout. What matters is the last clause of it: the activity is inspected regardless of which standard you name."

findings.problem: The definition of harm is given twice, once per chunk, with wording that drifts. Slide 16: "harm being injury or damage to health at 3.3." Slide 20: "a harm is physical injury or damage to health, at 3.3." One says injury, the other physical injury, four slides apart, both citing the same clause. The same doubling happens with the IEC 62366-1 bridge, described three times: slide 8 "the textual bridge between this standard and your usability engineering work", slide 23 "which is the bridge across to IEC 62366-1", slide 34 "which is why ISO 14971 takes the definition of use error at 3.30 from IEC 62366-1."
findings.fix: Define harm once, at slide 16, with the standard's own wording, and at slide 20 refer back ("a harm, as we defined it, is the injury itself"). Keep the bridge metaphor at slide 8 only; at slides 23 and 34 state the specific link without re-introducing the relationship.

findings.problem: A forward reference points one slide past its target. Slide 1: "Everything in this deck is sourced, and the last slide tells you what to re-verify before you rely on any of it." The sources and the verification band are on slide 38; slide 39 is the close and Q&A. Slide 34 has the mirror-image error: "This is the last content slide" — slide 37's ten-item list is content, and the room is told to keep the page.
findings.fix: Slide 1: "the sources slide near the end tells you what to re-verify." Slide 34: "This is the last slide of new material."

findings.problem: An acronym is expanded, never used, and then bypassed later. Slide 11: "a risk-based approach applied to the control of the appropriate Quality Management System (QMS) processes." QMS never appears again anywhere in the deck; slide 33 writes it out in full instead ("puts risk management inside the quality management system"). Conversely MDCG is used unexpanded three times (slide 12's "MDCG 2021-5 rev.1", slide 34's "MDCG 2025-10" and "MDCG 2019-16 revision 1") and only expanded at slide 38: "guidance from the Medical Device Coordination Group, or MDCG, is revised and superseded."
findings.fix: Drop the QMS expansion at slide 11 and say "quality management system" throughout. Move the MDCG expansion to its first use at slide 12 and use the short form at 34 and 38.

findings.problem: Every other interaction in the deck carries a bracketed capitalised cue on its own line, but the final and longest one does not. Slide 39 ends "I want to thank each of you who attended, and I welcome any questions you may have at this time" with no cue, where slides 2, 9, 15, 18, 28 and 36 all have one. The cue style also mixes numerals and words: "[TABLE WORK - 10 MINUTES. CIRCULATE.]" and "[TABLE WORK - 9 MINUTES. CIRCULATE.]" against "[FIVE MINUTES OF INDIVIDUAL WORK. CIRCULATE.]" and "[PAUSE WHILE THE ROOM FORMS GROUPS OF 3 OR 4]".
findings.fix: Add "[OPEN FOR QUESTIONS]" on its own line at the end of slide 39, and normalise durations inside cues to digits: "[5 MINUTES OF INDIVIDUAL WORK. CIRCULATE.]", "[PAUSE WHILE THE ROOM FORMS GROUPS OF 3 OR 4]".

summary:
Needs work. The deck's bones are good — the agenda arithmetic adds to 90, all three exercises are set up and resumed, every "so now that we have established" transition points at real prior material, and the close does echo the opening's "the file is the argument." The bracketed stage directions are genuinely consistent: all capitals, all on their own lines, none mistakable for speech. But the chunk seams show badly in five ways.

Deliverability failures that will be visible to the room in real time: slide 35 promises 8 minutes for Exercise C and slide 36 immediately says 5; slide 36 says "2 of them deliberately defective," lists 3 defects, then says "all 5 of those"; slide 36 calls the sixth of its six checks "the Clause 8 evaluation" when none of the six is about Clause 8; and slide 37 tells the room to do "the second one, the verification of effectiveness records" when that is item 3 on the page they are holding.

The worst continuity break is slide 16 handing over Exercise A's model answer — the compliant-fluid-path hazard and the fact that it splits into several rows — two slides before slide 18 promises "I am not going to pre-empt any of the findings."

Repetition is the dominant seam problem. The reviewer traversal is delivered as new three times (slides 2, 6, 30); "Clause 7 runs to 7.6, not to 7.5" appears verbatim at slides 7 and 24 along with the Clause 6 routing point; the Team-NB V4 citation, its April 2026 date and its pitfall list run near-verbatim at slides 14 and 30; MDR is expanded four times and GSPR three; and seven separate slides claim to be the one thing to take away, which cancels the actual close. Three unrelated sets of "four things" (slides 2, 5, 20/21) are each framed as the canonical four.

Speakability is weakest in the regulatory middle. Slide 14 has a 95-word sentence, slide 25 a 90-word eight-item list, and slides 33-34 speak roughly twenty citations including "85 FR 17584" and a numbering-trap sentence whose entire point requires the listener to hold "Sections 1 and 9" against "Sections 1 and 8" unseen. Slide 13 opens on "this distinction" with no antecedent yet spoken, and slide 20's "MDR reportable event" collides with the deck's 30-odd other uses of MDR six slides after the only warning.

Finally, the arc: slide 2 promises "I will come back to what this room has told me as we work" and never does, and slide 39 delivers its best line — "A risk file is an argument, not an archive" — then buries it under 350 words of FAQ, a disclaimer, and a 41-word closing sentence that inverts slide 11's own argument about the activity being what gets inspected.
